computer-basics.title: Introduction to Computers
computer-basics.summary: What a computer is, its types, uses and why it matters.
computer-basics.html:
What is a computer?

A computer is an electronic machine that accepts data (raw facts), processes it following a set of instructions, and produces useful information. It then stores that information for later use.

The four basic operations form the IPOS cycle:

  • Input — you enter data (typing, clicking, scanning).
  • Processing — the computer works on the data.
  • Output — results are shown (screen, printout, sound).
  • Storage — the work is saved for the future.

Characteristics of a computer

  • Speed — performs millions of operations in a second.
  • Accuracy — gives correct results (mistakes are usually human — "garbage in, garbage out").
  • Storage — keeps large amounts of data.
  • Diligence — never gets tired or bored.
  • Versatility — does many different tasks.

Types of computers

  • Desktop — a full computer for an office or home desk.
  • Laptop — portable, battery-powered, all-in-one.
  • Tablet & smartphone — touch-screen, pocket-sized computers.
  • Server — a powerful computer that serves many users/network.

Everyday uses

Computers are used in business (records, accounts), education (learning, research), banking (mobile money, ATMs), communication (email, WhatsApp), entertainment and government services.

Key points: A computer turns data into information through Input → Processing → Output → Storage. It is fast, accurate, tireless and versatile.

computer-basics.title: Computer Hardware
computer-basics.summary: The physical parts — processor, memory, storage and devices.
computer-basics.html:
What is hardware?

Hardware means the physical parts of a computer you can touch. It is grouped into the system unit, input devices, output devices and storage.

Inside the system unit

  • CPU (Central Processing Unit) — the "brain"; it carries out instructions. Speed is measured in GHz.
  • RAM (Random Access Memory) — temporary working memory. More RAM = smoother multitasking. It is volatile (cleared when power goes off).
  • Motherboard — the main board that connects all parts.
  • Storage drive (HDD/SSD) — keeps your files permanently. An SSD is much faster than an HDD.
  • Power supply — provides electricity to the parts.

Input devices

Used to enter data: keyboard, mouse, touchpad, scanner, microphone, webcam.

Output devices

Used to get results: monitor (screen), printer, speakers, projector.

Storage sizes (smallest → largest)

Bit → Byte → Kilobyte (KB) → Megabyte (MB) → Gigabyte (GB) → Terabyte (TB). 1024 of one unit makes the next.

Key points: CPU processes, RAM is temporary memory, the drive stores permanently. Input devices feed data in; output devices give results out.

computer-basics.title: Software & Operating Systems
computer-basics.summary: System vs application software and how Windows works.
computer-basics.html:
What is software?

Software is the set of instructions (programs) that tell the hardware what to do. Without software, hardware cannot do anything useful.

Two main types

  • System software — runs the computer itself. The most important is the Operating System (OS), e.g. Windows, macOS, Android.
  • Application software — programs you use for tasks: MS Word, Excel, browsers, WhatsApp, games.

What the Operating System does

  • Starts the computer (booting).
  • Manages files, memory and devices (printer, keyboard…).
  • Provides the screen you interact with (the desktop).
  • Runs your applications.

The Windows desktop

  • Desktop — the main screen after start-up.
  • Icons — small pictures that open programs or files.
  • Taskbar — the bar at the bottom (Start button, open programs, clock).
  • Windows — each program opens in a rectangle you can move, resize, minimise or close.
  • Start menu — where you find all your programs and the shut-down option.
Key points: System software (the OS) runs the machine; application software does your tasks. Always shut down properly from the Start menu.

computer-basics.title: Files, Folders & Storage
computer-basics.summary: Saving, organising and backing up your work safely.
computer-basics.html:
Files and folders

  • A file is a single saved item — a document, photo, song or video.
  • A folder is a container that holds files and other folders, to keep them organised.
  • Each file has a name and an extension that shows its type: .docx (Word), .pdf, .jpg (photo), .mp3 (music).

Common actions

  • Save — store your work (Ctrl + S). Save As — save a new copy with a new name.
  • Copy (Ctrl + C) and Paste (Ctrl + V) — duplicate a file.
  • Cut (Ctrl + X) and Paste — move a file.
  • Rename, Delete — deleted items go to the Recycle Bin (can be restored).

Storage devices

Save and carry files using: flash drives, memory cards, external hard drives, or cloud storage (Google Drive, OneDrive) which keeps files online.

Backups — protect your work

A backup is a second copy of your important files kept somewhere else (flash drive or cloud). If your computer is lost, stolen or damaged, your work is safe. Back up regularly.

Key points: Organise files into named folders, save often, and keep a backup. Remove flash drives safely to avoid losing data.

computer-basics.title: Word Processing (Microsoft Word)
computer-basics.summary: Create, format, and print professional documents.
computer-basics.html:
What is word processing?

Word processing is using a program like Microsoft Word to create text documents — letters, reports, CVs and notes.

Getting started

  • Open Word and start a Blank document.
  • Type your text. Press Enter to start a new paragraph.
  • Save early and often: Ctrl + S, give the file a clear name.

Formatting your text

  • Bold (Ctrl + B), Italic (Ctrl + I), Underline (Ctrl + U).
  • Change the font, size and colour from the Home tab.
  • Alignment: left, centre, right, justify.
  • Use bullet and numbered lists for points.

Adding more

  • Insert tab → add tables, pictures, page numbers and headers/footers.
  • Check spelling from the Review tab.

Printing

File → Print. Choose the printer, number of copies, then Print. Use Print Preview first to check how it will look.

Key points: Type, format neatly, save with Ctrl + S, and preview before printing. Practice by typing a simple letter.

computer-basics.title: The Internet & Email
computer-basics.summary: Browse, search, use email and stay safe online.
computer-basics.html:
The Internet

The Internet is a worldwide network that connects millions of computers, letting them share information. The World Wide Web is the collection of websites you visit.

Web browsers

A browser opens websites: Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Firefox. Type a web address (URL) or a search word in the address bar.

Searching with Google

  • Type clear keywords, not whole sentences.
  • Use quotation marks "…" to search an exact phrase.
  • Check that a source looks trustworthy before believing it.

Email

  • An email address looks like name@gmail.com.
  • Compose a message: add the recipient (To), a Subject, your message, then Send.
  • Attachments — send files (documents, photos) with your email.
  • CC/BCC — send a copy to others (BCC hides the addresses).

Staying safe online

  • Never share your password or PIN.
  • Beware of scams/phishing — messages that trick you into giving money or details.
  • For Mobile Money, always confirm the name before sending.
Key points: Use a browser to reach websites, search with keywords, and email with a clear subject. Protect your passwords and watch out for scams.

computer-basics.title: Computer Care & Security
computer-basics.summary: Protect against viruses, keep data safe, maintain your machine.
computer-basics.html:
Viruses and malware

A virus is a harmful program that can damage files or steal data. Malware is the general name for all harmful software.

Protecting your computer

  • Install and update antivirus software.
  • Don't open unknown email attachments or links.
  • Scan flash drives before using them.
  • Keep Windows and programs updated.
  • Use strong passwords and lock your screen when away.

Looking after the hardware

  • Keep the computer clean and free of dust.
  • Use a stable power source / surge protector; shut down properly.
  • Don't eat or drink over the keyboard.
  • Handle laptops gently; charge the battery correctly.

Good working habits (ergonomics)

Sit upright, keep the screen at eye level, and take short breaks to rest your eyes and hands.

Key points: Use antivirus, avoid unknown links, back up your data, keep software updated, and treat the hardware with care.

computer-basics.title: Practical Skills & Revision
computer-basics.summary: Typing practice, everyday tasks, and a revision checklist.
computer-basics.html:
Typing skills

  • Place fingers on the home row (ASDF — JKL;). Keep thumbs on the space bar.
  • Look at the screen, not the keys — build touch typing.
  • Accuracy first, then speed. Practice a little every day.

Everyday tasks to master

  • Turn the computer on and off correctly.
  • Create a folder, save a document into it, and find it again.
  • Copy files to a flash drive safely.
  • Type and format a one-page letter.
  • Create an email and send an attachment.

Revision checklist

  • Can you explain Input → Processing → Output → Storage?
  • Can you name the CPU, RAM and storage and their jobs?
  • Do you know the difference between system and application software?
  • Can you save, organise and back up your files?
  • Can you search the web and send an email safely?
Well done! Complete the course quiz to earn your certificate. Keep practising — the computer rewards the curious.

microsoft-office.title: Getting Started with Microsoft Office
microsoft-office.summary: The Office suite, the ribbon interface, and skills shared by every program.
microsoft-office.html:
What is Microsoft Office?

Microsoft Office is a suite (collection) of programs used for office and business work. The main programs are:

  • Word — word processing (letters, reports, CVs).
  • Excel — spreadsheets (numbers, calculations, charts).
  • PowerPoint — presentations (slides).
  • Access — databases (organised records).
  • Publisher — desktop publishing (flyers, cards, newsletters).

The common interface

All Office programs look similar, so learning one helps you learn the rest.

  • Ribbon — the strip of tools at the top, divided into tabs (Home, Insert, Layout…).
  • Quick Access Toolbar — small icons for Save, Undo, Redo.
  • File / Backstage — New, Open, Save, Print, and program options.
  • Status bar — information at the bottom (page number, zoom).

Skills used everywhere

  • Save (Ctrl + S) and Save As to a chosen folder; know the file types: .docx, .xlsx, .pptx, .accdb, .pub.
  • Open, New, Print (Ctrl + P).
  • Undo (Ctrl + Z) / Redo (Ctrl + Y).
  • Cut/Copy/Paste (Ctrl + X / C / V).
Key points: Office programs share the ribbon interface. Master Save, Open, Print, Undo and Copy/Paste once — they work in all of them.

microsoft-office.title: Microsoft Word — Word Processing
microsoft-office.summary: Create, format, lay out and finish professional documents.
microsoft-office.html:
Purpose

Word is used to create and edit text documents — letters, reports, CVs, notes and books.

Typing & editing

  • Type text; press Enter for a new paragraph.
  • Select text by dragging, then edit, delete or format it.
  • Find & Replace (Ctrl + H) to change words quickly.

Character formatting (Home tab)

Bold, Italic, Underline, font type, size, colour, highlight, superscript/subscript.

Paragraph formatting

  • Alignment: left, centre, right, justify.
  • Line and paragraph spacing; indents.
  • Bullets and numbered lists.

Styles & templates

Styles (Heading 1, Heading 2, Normal) format text consistently and build an automatic Table of Contents. Templates are ready-made designs.

Page layout

  • Margins, orientation (portrait/landscape), paper size, columns.
  • Headers & footers and automatic page numbers (Insert tab).
  • Page break (Ctrl + Enter) to start a new page.

Inserting objects

Insert tab: tables, pictures, shapes, SmartArt, symbols and hyperlinks.

Tables

Rows and columns of cells for data. Insert a table, add/delete rows, merge cells, and apply a table style.

References

Table of Contents, footnotes, captions and citations (References tab) — built from your Heading styles.

Mail Merge

Create many personalised letters/labels from one document + a list of names (Mailings tab): Start Mail Merge → select recipients → insert merge fields → finish & print.

Review & finishing

  • Spelling & Grammar check (Review tab).
  • Track Changes and Comments for editing together.
  • Print (Ctrl + P) — preview first, then print.
Key points: Format with styles, lay out pages with margins/headers, insert tables and pictures, and use Mail Merge for bulk letters. Always spell-check and preview before printing.

microsoft-office.title: Microsoft Excel — Spreadsheets
microsoft-office.summary: Enter data, calculate with formulas & functions, and make charts.
microsoft-office.html:
Purpose

Excel organises numbers and text in a grid and performs calculations automatically — budgets, records, marks, accounts.

The workbook

  • A file is a workbook; it contains worksheets (tabs at the bottom).
  • A sheet is a grid of cells. Columns are letters (A, B, C), rows are numbers (1, 2, 3), so a cell is A1, B4…

Entering data

Click a cell and type text, numbers or dates. Press Enter or Tab to move. Use AutoFill (drag the small corner handle) to continue a series.

Formulas

  • Every formula starts with =.
  • Operators: + − * / and ( ). Example: =(A1+B1)*2.
  • Reference cells, not typed numbers, so results update automatically.

Common functions

  • =SUM(A1:A10) — adds a range.
  • =AVERAGE(A1:A10) — mean.
  • =MAX / MIN / COUNT — highest, lowest, how many.
  • =IF(A1>=50,"Pass","Fail") — makes a decision.
  • =VLOOKUP(...) — looks up a value in a table.

Formatting

Number formats (currency UGX, percentage, date), borders, cell colours, merge & centre, wrap text, adjust row/column size.

Sorting & filtering

Sort data A→Z or by value; use Filter to show only rows that match a condition.

Charts

Select data → Insert → choose a column, bar, line or pie chart to show it visually.

Advanced

  • Conditional formatting — colour cells by rule (e.g. fails in red).
  • Data validation — drop-down lists to control entry.
  • Pivot tables — summarise large data quickly.

Printing

Set the print area, fit to page, add gridlines/headings if needed, then print.

Key points: Formulas start with =. Use SUM, AVERAGE and IF, reference cells so results auto-update, then present with charts. Sort/filter to analyse, pivot tables to summarise.

microsoft-office.title: Microsoft PowerPoint — Presentations
microsoft-office.summary: Build and deliver clear, attractive slide shows.
microsoft-office.html:
Purpose

PowerPoint creates presentations — a series of slides shown on a screen or projector to support a talk.

Slides & layouts

  • Add slides (New Slide) and choose a layout (Title, Title & Content, Two Content…).
  • Use placeholders for titles, text, pictures.
  • Manage slides in the left thumbnail pane (reorder, duplicate, delete).

Design & themes

Themes (Design tab) give consistent colours, fonts and backgrounds. The Slide Master lets you change the look of all slides at once (e.g. add a logo).

Content

  • Keep text short — a few bullet points, not paragraphs.
  • Insert pictures, shapes, SmartArt, charts, audio and video (Insert tab).

Transitions & animations

  • Transitions — the effect between slides.
  • Animations — effects on an object (appear, fly in). Use sparingly.

Delivering the show

  • Start: F5 (from beginning) or Shift + F5 (current slide).
  • Move with arrow keys / click; press Esc to end.
  • Presenter View shows your notes and the next slide on your screen while the audience sees only the slide.

Good practice

One idea per slide, large readable fonts, high-contrast colours, and rehearse your timing.

Key points: Use layouts and a theme for consistency, keep slides short and visual, add gentle transitions, and use Presenter View to deliver confidently.

microsoft-office.title: Microsoft Access — Databases
microsoft-office.summary: Store and manage large sets of related records.
microsoft-office.html:
Purpose

Access is a database program. A database stores large amounts of organised data — for example students, customers or stock — so it can be searched and reported on.

Key objects

  • Tables — store the data in rows (records) and columns (fields).
  • Queries — ask questions of the data (find, filter, calculate).
  • Forms — friendly screens for entering and viewing records.
  • Reports — neat, printable summaries of the data.

Designing a table

  • Each field has a data type: Short Text, Number, Date/Time, Currency, Yes/No, AutoNumber.
  • A Primary Key uniquely identifies each record (e.g. StudentID) — no duplicates.

Relationships

Tables are linked using matching key fields (e.g. a Students table and a Marks table share StudentID). This is a relational database and avoids repeating data.

Queries

Use Design View to choose fields and set criteria (e.g. Class = "S1"). Queries can sort, filter and calculate totals.

Forms & Reports

  • Forms make data entry easier and reduce mistakes.
  • Reports group, sort and total data for printing (e.g. a class list or invoice).
Key points: A database is built from Tables (data), Queries (questions), Forms (entry) and Reports (output). Give each table a Primary Key and link related tables with relationships.

microsoft-office.title: Microsoft Publisher — Desktop Publishing
microsoft-office.summary: Design flyers, cards, brochures and newsletters.
microsoft-office.html:
Purpose

Publisher is a desktop publishing program used to design printed materials with precise layout — business cards, flyers, brochures, certificates, calendars and newsletters. It gives more layout control than Word.

Starting a publication

  • Choose a template (Business Card, Flyer, Brochure…) or a blank page of the right size.
  • Set the page size and orientation for your job.

Working with objects

  • Everything sits in text boxes and picture boxes you can place anywhere.
  • Move, resize, rotate, align and layer (bring to front / send to back) objects.
  • Use guides and snapping for neat alignment.

Design tools

  • Building Blocks — ready-made borders, calendars and adverts.
  • Colour schemes and font schemes for a consistent brand look.
  • Insert your logo and pictures.

Common publications

  • Business cards & letterheads — small, exact layouts.
  • Flyers & posters — one eye-catching page.
  • Brochures — folded, multi-panel documents.
  • Newsletters — multi-page with columns and headings.

Printing & sharing

Check the layout, then print — or save/export as PDF to send to a printing bureau.

Key points: Publisher uses movable text and picture boxes for precise design. Start from a template, keep colours/fonts consistent, and export to PDF for professional printing.

internet-email.title: Understanding the Internet
internet-email.summary: What the Internet is, how you connect, and key terms.
internet-email.html:
What is the Internet?

The Internet is a global network that connects millions of computers so they can share information. The World Wide Web (WWW) is the huge collection of websites you visit on it.

How you connect

  • Mobile data — a SIM/bundle from a network (MTN, Airtel).
  • Wi-Fi — wireless internet from a router or hotspot.
  • Modem/router — the device that provides the connection.
  • An ISP (Internet Service Provider) supplies the service.

Key terms

  • Website — a set of related web pages (e.g. onlinetechug.com).
  • URL — a web address, e.g. https://www.onlinetechug.com.
  • Download — bring a file from the internet to your device; Upload — send one out.
  • Bandwidth/data — the amount of information you can send/receive.
Key points: The Internet connects computers worldwide; the Web is the websites on it. You connect through data or Wi-Fi via an ISP, and reach sites using their URL.

internet-email.title: Web Browsers & Searching
internet-email.summary: Use a browser well and find what you need on Google.
internet-email.html:
Web browsers

A browser is the program that opens websites — Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Firefox. Type a URL or search word in the address bar at the top.

Browser skills

  • Tabs — open several pages at once.
  • Bookmarks/Favourites — save sites you visit often.
  • History — pages you've visited; Back/Forward arrows to move.
  • Refresh to reload; Downloads folder holds files you save.

Searching with Google

  • Type clear keywords, not full sentences (e.g. price of laptop in Uganda).
  • Use quotation marks "…" for an exact phrase.
  • Add words to narrow results; scan the short descriptions before clicking.
  • Prefer trusted sources; be careful of adverts dressed as results.

Downloading & uploading

Click a download link to save a file; use an Upload/Attach button to send a file (e.g. a photo or CV) to a website.

Key points: The browser opens websites; use tabs, bookmarks and history to work faster. Search with keywords and check that sources are trustworthy.

internet-email.title: Email — Sending & Receiving
internet-email.summary: Create an account and send professional messages with attachments.
internet-email.html:
What is email?

Email (electronic mail) sends written messages and files between people over the internet. A common free service is Gmail.

Your email address

It looks like yourname@gmail.com — the part before @ is your name, after @ is the provider. To create one: go to Gmail → Create account → follow the steps → set a strong password.

Sending a message (Compose)

  • To — the recipient's address.
  • Subject — a short line saying what it's about.
  • Body — your message; be clear and polite.
  • Send — deliver it.

CC, BCC and attachments

  • CC — send a copy to others (everyone sees the addresses).
  • BCC — copy others privately (addresses hidden).
  • Attachment — click the 📎 to send a file (document, photo).

Managing your inbox

  • Inbox — received mail; Sent — mail you sent.
  • Reply, Reply All, Forward.
  • Use labels/folders and search to stay organised; delete or archive old mail.
Key points: An email needs a recipient, a subject and a message. Use attachments for files, CC/BCC to copy others, and keep your inbox tidy with labels.

internet-email.title: Online Safety, Scams & Mobile Money
internet-email.summary: Protect yourself, spot scams, and transact safely.
internet-email.html:
Protect your accounts

  • Use strong passwords (letters, numbers, symbols) and a different one per account.
  • Never share your password, PIN or OTP — no genuine company asks for them.
  • Turn on two-step verification where possible.
  • Log out on shared/public computers.

Spotting scams (phishing)

  • Messages that create panic or urgency ("your account will close!").
  • Fake "you have won" prizes asking you to pay or click a link.
  • Links that look slightly wrong; check the real web address.
  • Requests to send money or airtime to "help" someone.

Mobile Money safety

  • Always confirm the recipient's name before approving.
  • Keep your PIN secret; don't approve prompts you didn't start.
  • Ignore "wrong send, please reverse" tricks — verify first.
  • Keep the SMS confirmation as your receipt.

Video calls & communication

Stay in touch with WhatsApp, Zoom and Google Meet for messages, voice and video calls — useful for work, school and family.

Key points: Guard your passwords and PIN, never trust urgent "prize/reverse" messages, and always confirm the name before sending Mobile Money.

typing-skills.title: The Keyboard & Correct Posture
typing-skills.summary: Know the keyboard layout and set up to type without strain.
typing-skills.html:
The keyboard layout

Standard keyboards use the QWERTY layout (named after the first six letters). Main areas:

  • Letter keys — the middle block.
  • Number row — across the top; numeric keypad on the right (on full keyboards).
  • Function keys — F1–F12 along the top.
  • Special keys — Enter, Backspace, Shift, Ctrl, Alt, Caps Lock, Tab, Space bar.

Posture & set-up

  • Sit upright, feet flat, back supported.
  • Screen at eye level, about an arm's length away.
  • Wrists straight and relaxed — don't rest them hard on the desk.
  • Good light to avoid eye strain.
Key points: Learn the QWERTY layout and the special keys, and set up with good posture — it prevents fatigue and helps you type faster.

typing-skills.title: Touch Typing — Home Row & Finger Placement
typing-skills.summary: The correct finger positions for typing without looking.
typing-skills.html:
The home row

Touch typing means typing without looking at the keys. You start from the home row:

  • Left hand fingers on A S D F; right hand on J K L ;
  • Both thumbs rest on the Space bar.
  • F and J have small bumps so you can find home without looking.

Which finger types which key

  • Each finger reaches the keys just above and below its home key.
  • Always return to the home row after each keystroke.
  • Use the Shift key with the opposite hand for capital letters.

Practice tips

  • Keep your eyes on the screen, not the keyboard.
  • Start slowly and correctly — speed comes with time.
  • Practise the home row first, then add top and bottom rows.
Key points: Rest fingers on ASDF–JKL;, feel the F and J bumps, and always return to home. Type without looking — accuracy before speed.

typing-skills.title: Building Accuracy & Speed
typing-skills.summary: Drills and habits that grow correct, fast typing.
typing-skills.html:
Accuracy first

Typing correctly matters more than typing fast. Mistakes waste time. Build accuracy, then speed will follow naturally.

Daily drills

  • Practise the same keys until they feel automatic (muscle memory).
  • Type common words and short phrases repeatedly.
  • Add numbers, capitals and punctuation gradually.
  • Use a free typing tutor or website for guided lessons.

Measuring progress (WPM)

  • WPM = Words Per Minute — your typing speed.
  • Beginners ~20 WPM; steady practice reaches 40–60+ WPM.
  • Take a typing test weekly to track improvement.

Useful shortcuts

Ctrl + C (copy), Ctrl + V (paste), Ctrl + Z (undo), Ctrl + S (save) — they speed up all your work.

Key points: Practise a little every day, aim for accuracy first, build muscle memory, and track your WPM. Learn shortcuts to work faster.

microsoft-word.title: Word Basics — Typing & Editing
microsoft-word.summary: The Word screen, entering text, and editing.
microsoft-word.html:
What is Microsoft Word?

Word is a word-processing program used to create text documents — letters, reports, CVs, notes and books.

The Word screen

  • Ribbon — tabs of tools (Home, Insert, Layout…).
  • Document area — the blank page you type on.
  • Cursor — the blinking line where text appears.
  • Status bar — page and word count at the bottom.

Typing & editing

  • Type text; press Enter for a new paragraph, Space between words.
  • Backspace deletes left, Delete deletes right.
  • Select text by dragging, then edit, delete or format it.
  • Undo (Ctrl + Z) / Redo (Ctrl + Y).
  • Find & Replace (Ctrl + H) to change words quickly.

Saving & opening

Save with Ctrl + S (file type .docx); give a clear name and choose a folder. Use File → Open to reopen work later.

Key points: Word creates text documents. Type, edit with Backspace/Delete, undo mistakes, and save early with Ctrl + S.

microsoft-word.title: Formatting & Styles
microsoft-word.summary: Make documents neat with fonts, paragraphs, lists and styles.
microsoft-word.html:
Character formatting (Home tab)

Bold (Ctrl + B), Italic (Ctrl + I), Underline (Ctrl + U). Change the font, size, colour and highlight.

Paragraph formatting

  • Alignment: left, centre, right, justify.
  • Line and paragraph spacing; indents.
  • Bullet and numbered lists for points.

Styles & templates

Styles (Heading 1, Heading 2, Normal) keep formatting consistent and let Word build an automatic Table of Contents. Templates are ready-made designs (CV, letter…).

Key points: Format characters (bold, font, colour) and paragraphs (alignment, spacing, lists). Use Heading styles for a consistent, professional look.

microsoft-word.title: Layout, Tables, Pictures, Mail Merge & Printing
microsoft-word.summary: Page setup, objects, bulk letters and finishing your document.
microsoft-word.html:
Page layout

  • Margins, orientation (portrait/landscape), paper size, columns.
  • Headers & footers and automatic page numbers (Insert tab).
  • Page break (Ctrl + Enter) to start a new page.

Tables & pictures

Insert tab → add tables (rows & columns of cells), pictures, shapes and SmartArt. Add/delete rows, merge cells, apply table styles.

Mail Merge

Create many personalised letters or labels from one document + a list of names (Mailings tab): Start Mail Merge → select recipients → insert merge fields → finish & print.

Review & printing

  • Spelling & Grammar check and Track Changes/Comments (Review tab).
  • Print (Ctrl + P) — preview first, choose copies, then print.
Key points: Set page layout, insert tables/pictures, use Mail Merge for bulk letters, and always spell-check and preview before printing.

microsoft-excel.title: Excel Basics — Workbook, Cells & Data
microsoft-excel.summary: The spreadsheet grid and entering data.
microsoft-excel.html:
What is Excel?

Excel is a spreadsheet program that organises numbers and text in a grid and calculates automatically — budgets, records, marks, accounts.

Workbooks & worksheets

  • A file is a workbook (.xlsx); it holds worksheets (tabs at the bottom).
  • A sheet is a grid of cells. Columns are letters (A, B, C), rows are numbers (1, 2, 3) — a cell is A1, B4…

Entering data

  • Click a cell and type text, numbers or dates. Press Enter or Tab to move.
  • Use AutoFill (drag the small corner handle) to continue a series (1, 2, 3… or Jan, Feb…).
  • Adjust column width/row height by dragging the borders.
Key points: A workbook holds worksheets of cells named by column letter + row number. Type data, then AutoFill to continue a series quickly.

microsoft-excel.title: Formulas & Functions
microsoft-excel.summary: Calculate automatically with =, SUM, AVERAGE, IF and VLOOKUP.
microsoft-excel.html:
Formulas

  • Every formula starts with =.
  • Operators: + − * / and ( ). Example: =(A1+B1)*2.
  • Reference cells (A1, B2), not typed numbers, so results update automatically when data changes.

Common functions

  • =SUM(A1:A10) — adds a range.
  • =AVERAGE(A1:A10) — the mean.
  • =MAX / =MIN / =COUNT — highest, lowest, how many.
  • =IF(A1>=50,"Pass","Fail") — makes a decision.
  • =VLOOKUP(...) — looks up a value in a table.
Key points: Formulas start with =. Use SUM, AVERAGE and IF, and reference cells so results recalculate on their own.

microsoft-excel.title: Formatting, Sort/Filter, Charts & Printing
microsoft-excel.summary: Present and analyse data, then print it well.
microsoft-excel.html:
Formatting

Number formats (currency UGX, percentage, date), borders, cell colours, merge & centre, wrap text. Conditional formatting colours cells by rule (e.g. fails in red).

Sorting & filtering

Sort A→Z or by value; use Filter to show only rows that match a condition. Data validation creates drop-down lists.

Charts

Select data → Insert → choose a column, bar, line or pie chart to show it visually. Pivot tables summarise large data quickly.

Printing

Set the print area, fit to page, add gridlines/headings if needed, then print.

Key points: Format for clarity, sort/filter to analyse, chart to present, and set the print area before printing.

microsoft-powerpoint.title: Slides, Layouts & Themes
microsoft-powerpoint.summary: Build the structure and look of a presentation.
microsoft-powerpoint.html:
What is PowerPoint?

PowerPoint creates presentations — a series of slides shown on a screen or projector to support a talk.

Slides & layouts

  • Add slides (New Slide) and choose a layout (Title, Title & Content, Two Content…).
  • Use placeholders for titles, text and pictures.
  • Manage slides in the left thumbnail pane — reorder, duplicate, delete.

Design & themes

Themes (Design tab) give consistent colours, fonts and backgrounds across all slides.

Key points: A presentation is a set of slides. Pick a layout for each and one theme for the whole deck to keep it consistent.

microsoft-powerpoint.title: Content, Transitions & Animations
microsoft-powerpoint.summary: Add text, media and gentle movement.
microsoft-powerpoint.html:
Adding content

  • Keep text short — a few bullet points, not paragraphs.
  • Insert pictures, shapes, SmartArt, charts, audio and video (Insert tab).

Transitions & animations

  • Transitions — the effect between slides.
  • Animations — effects on an object (appear, fly in). Use them sparingly.
Key points: One idea per slide, mostly visuals with short text. Add subtle transitions/animations — don't overdo them.

microsoft-powerpoint.title: Slide Master, Presenter View & Delivering
microsoft-powerpoint.summary: Brand every slide and present with confidence.
microsoft-powerpoint.html:
Slide Master

The Slide Master (View tab) changes the look of all slides at once — add a logo, set fonts and colours in one place.

Delivering the show

  • Start: F5 (from beginning) or Shift + F5 (current slide).
  • Move with arrow keys / click; press Esc to end.
  • Presenter View shows your notes and the next slide on your screen while the audience sees only the slide.

Good practice

Large readable fonts, high-contrast colours, and rehearse your timing.

Key points: Use the Slide Master to brand all slides, start with F5, and use Presenter View to deliver smoothly.

microsoft-access.title: Databases & Tables
microsoft-access.summary: What a database is and how to store data in tables.
microsoft-access.html:
What is Access?

Access is a database program. A database stores large amounts of organised data — students, customers, stock — so it can be searched and reported on.

The four objects

  • Tables — store the data.
  • Queries — ask questions of the data.
  • Forms — screens for entering/viewing records.
  • Reports — printable summaries.

Designing a table

  • Rows are records; columns are fields.
  • Each field has a data type: Short Text, Number, Date/Time, Currency, Yes/No, AutoNumber.
  • A Primary Key uniquely identifies each record (e.g. StudentID) — no duplicates.
Key points: A database is built from Tables, Queries, Forms and Reports. Tables hold records (rows) and fields (columns); give each table a Primary Key.

microsoft-access.title: Relationships & Queries
microsoft-access.summary: Link tables and ask questions of your data.
microsoft-access.html:
Relationships

Tables are linked using matching key fields (e.g. a Students table and a Marks table share StudentID). This is a relational database and avoids repeating data.

Queries

  • Use Design View to choose fields and set criteria (e.g. Class = "S1").
  • Queries can sort, filter and calculate totals.
  • Save a query and re-run it any time on the latest data.
Key points: Relationships link tables through shared key fields; queries find, filter and calculate answers from the data.

microsoft-access.title: Forms & Reports
microsoft-access.summary: Enter data easily and produce neat printouts.
microsoft-access.html:
Forms

Forms are friendly screens for entering and viewing one record at a time. They make data entry easier and reduce mistakes.

Reports

Reports present data neatly for printing — they can group, sort and total records (e.g. a class list, an invoice, a stock report).

Key points: Use Forms for tidy data entry and Reports for professional, printable summaries of your data.

microsoft-publisher.title: Publisher Basics & Publications
microsoft-publisher.summary: What Publisher does and how to start a design.
microsoft-publisher.html:
What is Publisher?

Publisher is a desktop-publishing program for designing printed materials with precise layout — business cards, flyers, brochures, certificates, calendars and newsletters. It gives more layout control than Word.

Starting a publication

  • Choose a template (Business Card, Flyer, Brochure…) or a blank page of the right size.
  • Set the page size and orientation for your job.
Key points: Publisher is for precise print designs. Start from a template or set the exact page size for your publication.

microsoft-publisher.title: Text & Picture Boxes, Design
microsoft-publisher.summary: Place and style objects for a neat, branded look.
microsoft-publisher.html:
Working with objects

  • Everything sits in movable text boxes and picture boxes.
  • Move, resize, rotate, align and layer (bring to front / send to back).
  • Use guides and snapping for neat alignment.

Design tools

  • Building Blocks — ready-made borders, calendars and adverts.
  • Colour schemes and font schemes for a consistent brand look.
  • Insert your logo and pictures.
Key points: Publisher uses movable text and picture boxes. Align with guides and keep colours/fonts consistent for a professional look.

microsoft-publisher.title: Common Publications & Printing
microsoft-publisher.summary: Design real items and prepare them for print.
microsoft-publisher.html:
Common publications

  • Business cards & letterheads — small, exact layouts.
  • Flyers & posters — one eye-catching page.
  • Brochures — folded, multi-panel documents.
  • Newsletters — multi-page with columns and headings.

Printing & sharing

Check the layout, then print — or save/export as PDF to send to a printing bureau.

Key points: Design cards, flyers, brochures and newsletters, then export to PDF for professional printing.

graphic-design.title: Design Foundations & Tools
graphic-design.summary: What graphic design is, the tools you'll use, and how designers work.
graphic-design.html:
What is graphic design?

Graphic design is visual communication — using images, type and colour to pass a message. A good design is not just "beautiful"; it makes the message clear, quick to understand and memorable.

Where design is used in business

  • Logos — the face of a brand.
  • Flyers & posters — promotions, events, shop offers.
  • Social media posts — Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, WhatsApp status.
  • Packaging & branding — labels, business cards, banners.

The three tools you will learn

  • Canva — free, browser-based, fastest for flyers and social posts. Best for beginners.
  • Adobe Photoshop — for photos: retouching, removing backgrounds, posters with images.
  • Adobe Illustrator — for vectors: logos and artwork that can scale to any size without blurring.

Raster vs vector — the most important concept

A raster image (JPG, PNG, photos) is made of tiny dots called pixels. Enlarge it too much and it becomes blurry. A vector (AI, SVG, EPS) is made of mathematical lines, so it stays razor-sharp at any size — from a business card to a billboard.

Rule: Always design a logo in a vector program (Illustrator). A client will eventually ask for it on a banner.

How professional designers work

1. Brief — understand what the client wants and who the audience is. 2. Sketch — rough ideas on paper first; it's faster than the computer. 3. Design — build it digitally. 4. Review — get feedback and revise. 5. Deliver — export the right file formats.

graphic-design.title: Design Principles That Make Work Look Professional
graphic-design.summary: Balance, contrast, hierarchy, alignment and whitespace.
graphic-design.html:
Why amateur designs look 'off'

Most poor designs break the same few rules. Learn these five and your work immediately looks more professional.

1. Visual hierarchy

The viewer should know what to read first. Make the most important thing (the offer, the headline) biggest and boldest. Supporting details are smaller. If everything shouts, nothing is heard.

2. Contrast

Contrast makes things stand out — dark text on a light background, a big heading next to small body text, a bright button on a calm background. Low contrast = hard to read, especially on phones and when printed.

3. Alignment

Every element should line up with something else. Pick a left edge and stick to it. Randomly placed text is the fastest way to look unprofessional. Use guides and grids.

4. Proximity (grouping)

Related items belong close together; unrelated items get space between them. A price should sit near its product, not floating across the page.

5. Whitespace

Whitespace (empty space) is not wasted space — it gives the design room to breathe and makes it feel premium. Beginners cram; professionals leave space.

Quick test: Squint at your design. Whatever you still notice is your hierarchy. If nothing stands out, fix it.

graphic-design.title: Colour & Typography
graphic-design.summary: Choosing colours that work together and fonts that stay readable.
graphic-design.html:
Understanding colour

Colours carry meaning: blue = trust (banks, tech), green = growth/money/health, red = urgency/sale, orange = friendly and energetic, black = luxury.

Building a palette

A safe formula is 60-30-10: 60% a dominant/background colour, 30% a secondary colour, 10% an accent for buttons and highlights. Two or three colours is usually enough — beginners use too many.

RGB vs CMYK — do not mix these up

  • RGB (Red Green Blue) — for anything on a screen: social media, websites.
  • CMYK (Cyan Magenta Yellow Black) — for anything printed: flyers, banners, cards.

If you design in RGB and print it, colours can come out duller than expected. Set your document to CMYK from the start for print jobs.

Typography basics

A typeface is the design (Arial, Georgia); a font is a specific weight/size of it. Two families:

  • Serif (Times, Georgia) — small "feet" on letters. Traditional, trustworthy.
  • Sans-serif (Arial, Helvetica, Montserrat) — clean, modern, best for screens.

Font rules that matter

  • Use two fonts maximum — one for headings, one for body.
  • Pair a bold display font with a simple readable one.
  • Never stretch or squash type — it looks distorted.
  • Keep body text large enough to read on a phone.
Safe pairing: Montserrat (headings) + Open Sans (body). Works for almost any business.

graphic-design.title: Logos, Branding & Exporting Your Work
graphic-design.summary: Designing a real logo and delivering the right files.
graphic-design.html:
What makes a strong logo

  • Simple — recognisable in one second.
  • Memorable — a distinctive shape or idea.
  • Versatile — works small (app icon) and large (banner).
  • Works in black and white — if it only works in colour, it's weak.
  • Appropriate — fits the industry.

Types of logo

Wordmark (just the name, like Google), lettermark (initials, like HP), icon/symbol (a mark), or a combination (icon + name) — the most useful for small businesses.

Building a brand kit

Deliver more than a logo. A brand kit contains: the logo in several versions (full colour, white, black), the colour codes (HEX for screen, CMYK for print), the fonts, and simple rules for spacing and misuse.

Exporting: the right file for the job

  • JPG — photos, social posts. Small size, no transparency.
  • PNG — when you need a transparent background (logos on websites).
  • PDF — sending to a printer; keeps quality and layout.
  • SVG / AI / EPS — vector master files. Always give the client these.

Resolution

72 DPI is fine for screens. 300 DPI is required for printing — anything less looks pixelated on paper. Set this when you create the document, not after.

Client tip: Deliver a folder with print files, web files and the editable master. It looks professional and prevents "can you resend it bigger?" messages.

digital-marketing.title: Digital Marketing Foundations
digital-marketing.summary: What digital marketing is, the main channels, and how to plan.
digital-marketing.html:
What is digital marketing?

Digital marketing is promoting a product or service using the internet — social media, search, email, WhatsApp and websites. Unlike a radio advert, you can measure exactly what worked and target only the people likely to buy.

The main channels

  • Social media — Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, X. Best for awareness and community.
  • WhatsApp Business — the highest-converting channel in Uganda; people already live there.
  • Search (SEO & Google) — reaching people actively looking for what you sell.
  • Paid ads — fast reach for money.
  • Email — cheap, owned, great for repeat customers.

Know your customer first

Before posting anything, answer: Who exactly are they (age, location, income)? What problem do they have? Where do they spend time online? What would make them trust you? Marketing to "everyone" reaches no one.

The marketing funnel

Awareness (they discover you) → Interest (they follow / ask) → Decision (they compare) → Action (they buy) → Loyalty (they return and refer). Each stage needs different content: entertaining at the top, proof and offers at the bottom.

Common mistake: Posting only "Buy now!" That is bottom-funnel content shown to people who don't know you yet. Mix in helpful and entertaining posts.

digital-marketing.title: Social Media & Content That Sells
digital-marketing.summary: Building pages, creating content and growing an audience.
digital-marketing.html:
Setting up properly

Use a clear profile photo (your logo), a cover image, and a bio that states what you sell, where you are, and how to order. Add your WhatsApp link. Many businesses lose sales simply because the contact method is hidden.

The content mix

Follow roughly 80/20: 80% value (tips, behind-the-scenes, customer stories, education) and 20% direct selling. Value content earns the attention that makes your sales posts work.

Content types that perform

  • Short videos / reels — highest reach on almost every platform right now.
  • Before & after — powerful for repairs, design and services.
  • Customer testimonials — screenshots of happy messages build trust fast.
  • Product close-ups — good lighting, clean background.
  • Answering real questions — every customer question is a post idea.

Writing captions that convert

Hook in the first line (people only see one line before "more"). Keep it short. Always end with a clear call to action: "WhatsApp us on 07xx to order today."

WhatsApp Business

Set up your catalogue, a greeting message, quick replies for common questions, and labels to track who is a new lead versus a paid customer. Post offers to your Status — it is free reach to people who already know you.

Consistency beats perfection. Three good posts every week outperform twenty posts one week and silence the next.

digital-marketing.title: Paid Ads & Measuring Results
digital-marketing.summary: Running ads that make money and reading the numbers.
digital-marketing.html:
Why run paid ads?

Organic reach is limited and slow. Ads let you put your offer in front of exactly the right people — by location, age, interests and behaviour — starting from a small daily budget.

Anatomy of a good ad

  • Attention-grabbing visual — video or a bright, clear image.
  • Clear offer — what they get and why now.
  • Trust signal — a price, a guarantee, or a testimonial.
  • One call to action — "Send WhatsApp message" works very well locally.

Targeting

Start narrow: your city plus a radius, the right age range, and one or two relevant interests. Broad targeting wastes money for small budgets. Once something works, scale the budget slowly.

The numbers that matter

  • Reach — how many people saw it.
  • Engagement — likes, comments, shares.
  • Clicks / CTR — how many acted. Under 1% usually means a weak creative or wrong audience.
  • Cost per result — the real one. What did each message or sale cost you?
  • ROI — money earned versus money spent. If you spend 100,000 and earn 400,000, keep going.

Testing

Never bet everything on one ad. Run 2–3 versions with different images or headlines on a small budget, then put the money behind the winner. This is how professionals lower costs over time.

Track every sale's source. Simply asking "how did you hear about us?" tells you where to spend more.

cybersecurity-basics.title: Security Foundations & Passwords
cybersecurity-basics.summary: The threats that matter and how to lock your accounts properly.
cybersecurity-basics.html:
Why this matters

Most people are not hacked by a genius — they are caught by simple, avoidable mistakes: a reused password, a fake link, an unlocked phone. Security is mostly habits, not expensive software.

The CIA triad

Security professionals protect three things: Confidentiality (only the right people see data), Integrity (data is not secretly changed), and Availability (you can access it when needed). A ransomware attack breaks all three.

What attackers actually want

  • Money — mobile money, bank details, ransom payments.
  • Accounts — to scam your friends and contacts from your name.
  • Data — customer lists, photos, documents for blackmail.

Strong passwords

Length beats complexity. A passphrase like BluePlate-Coffee-77 is stronger and easier to remember than P@ss1. Rules:

  • Never reuse a password across accounts. One leak then opens everything.
  • Use a password manager to store unique passwords for every site.
  • Change a password immediately if a service reports a breach.

Two-factor authentication (2FA)

2FA requires something you know (password) plus something you have (a code on your phone). Even if a thief has your password, they cannot get in. Turn it on for email first — your email can reset every other account.

Never share an OTP. No bank, telecom or company will ever ask for your one-time code or PIN. Anyone who does is a thief.

cybersecurity-basics.title: Phishing, Scams & Malware
cybersecurity-basics.summary: Spotting the traps and knowing what to do when infected.
cybersecurity-basics.html:
Phishing — the number one threat

Phishing is a fake message pretending to be someone you trust, designed to make you click, log in, or pay. It arrives by SMS, email, WhatsApp or a phone call.

How to spot it

  • Urgency and fear — "Your account will be closed today!" Panic stops people thinking.
  • Too good to be true — you won a promotion you never entered.
  • Wrong sender address — check the actual email domain, not the display name.
  • Odd links — hover to see the real destination before clicking.
  • Requests for PIN, password or OTP — always a scam.

Common local scams

"Wrong send" mobile money refunds, fake job offers asking for a registration fee, fake online shops, and impersonation of a boss or relative asking for urgent money. Verify by calling the person on a number you already know.

Types of malware

  • Virus — attaches to files and spreads.
  • Ransomware — encrypts your files and demands payment.
  • Spyware / keylogger — silently records what you type, including passwords.
  • Trojan — pretends to be useful software (a "free" cracked program).

How infections spread here

Overwhelmingly through flash drives, pirated/cracked software, and downloads from unofficial sites. Scan every USB drive before opening it, and install software only from official sources.

If infected: disconnect from the internet, do not pay the ransom, scan with a trusted antivirus, and restore from backup. Paying funds the criminals and rarely returns your files.

cybersecurity-basics.title: Protecting Your Data & Business
cybersecurity-basics.summary: Backups, safe browsing, privacy and securing a small business.
cybersecurity-basics.html:
Backups — your real insurance

Backup is the only reliable protection against ransomware, theft and hardware failure. Follow the 3-2-1 rule: 3 copies of important data, on 2 different types of storage, with 1 copy off-site (cloud or another building).

Automate it. A backup you must remember to run is a backup that will not exist when you need it. Test a restore occasionally — an unverified backup is only a hope.

Safe browsing

  • Look for https:// and the padlock before entering any password or card details.
  • Keep your browser and operating system updated — updates patch known holes.
  • Be careful on public Wi-Fi; avoid banking on it, or use a VPN.
  • Install browser extensions sparingly — they can read everything you do.

Privacy on social media

Oversharing helps attackers. Birthdays, pet names and school names are common security-question answers. Avoid posting travel plans in real time, and review who can see your posts and friend list.

Securing a small business

  • Separate accounts — each employee gets their own login. Never share one password.
  • Least privilege — staff access only what their job needs.
  • Remove access immediately when someone leaves.
  • Train your team — most breaches start with one careless click.
  • Secure the Wi-Fi — strong password, change the router's default admin login, keep a separate guest network.
Plan for the bad day. Write down: who to call, how to restore backups, and how to inform customers. A calm plan limits the damage.

web-development.title: How the Web Actually Works
web-development.summary: Clients, servers, HTTP, domains and hosting — the ground every web developer stands on.
web-development.html:
The client and the server

Every time you open a website, two machines talk. Your phone or laptop is the client; it asks for a page. Somewhere else a server — a computer that never sleeps — receives that request and sends back files. Web development is writing what the server sends and what the client does with it.

What happens when you type a web address

  1. You type onlinetechug.com.
  2. DNS (the internet's phone book) turns that name into an IP address like 102.23.11.4.
  3. Your browser opens a connection to that address and sends an HTTP request.
  4. The server replies with HTML, CSS, JavaScript and images.
  5. The browser assembles them and paints the page.
Why this matters: almost every bug you will ever debug lives in one of those five steps. Knowing them tells you where to look.

HTTP methods and status codes

Requests have a method: GET fetches something, POST sends new data (a form), PUT updates, DELETE removes. Responses carry a status code:

  • 200 — OK, here is your page.
  • 301 / 302 — moved; go here instead.
  • 404 — not found (the address is wrong).
  • 500 — the server itself broke. That one is your fault as a developer.

Front end vs back end

  • Front end — everything the user sees and clicks: HTML, CSS, JavaScript.
  • Back end — what runs on the server: PHP, Python, Node.js, plus the database.
  • Full stack — both. That is what this course builds towards.

Domains and hosting

A domain is the name you rent each year. Hosting is the computer your files live on. They are separate purchases, often from different companies, and you connect them by pointing the domain's nameservers at the host.

HTTPS encrypts traffic between client and server. It needs an SSL certificate — free ones from Let's Encrypt are standard now. Never take payments or passwords on a site without it.

web-development.title: HTML — The Structure of a Page
web-development.summary: Elements, semantic markup, forms and accessibility.
web-development.html:
What HTML is

HTML (HyperText Markup Language) is not a programming language — it has no logic. It describes structure: this is a heading, this is a paragraph, this is a list. The browser decides how to draw it.

Anatomy of an element

An element is an opening tag, content, and a closing tag: <p>Hello</p>. Tags can carry attributes that add information: <a href="/shop">Shop</a>. A few elements are self-closing, like <img src="laptop.jpg" alt="HP laptop">.

The skeleton of every page

Every document has a <head> (information about the page — title, description, links to stylesheets; none of it visible) and a <body> (everything the visitor sees).

Semantic HTML — and why it pays

You could build an entire site from <div>. Don't. Use tags that state meaning: <header>, <nav>, <main>, <article>, <footer>, <h1>–<h6>.

  • Search engines read structure to understand your page — it is free SEO.
  • Screen readers use it to let blind users navigate.
  • Other developers (including you in six months) can follow it.
Rule: one <h1> per page, and never skip heading levels to get a smaller font — that is CSS's job.

Forms — where data enters your site

A form collects input and sends it somewhere: <form action="/subscribe" method="post">. Inside it, <input>, <textarea>, <select> and <button>.

Always pair an input with a <label>. Use the right type — email, tel, number, password — because phones show a matching keyboard and browsers validate for free.

Accessibility basics

  • Every image needs alt text describing it (empty alt="" if purely decorative).
  • Links should say where they go — "Read our delivery policy", not "click here".
  • Everything clickable must be reachable with the Tab key.

web-development.title: CSS — Making It Look Right
web-development.summary: The box model, layout with Flexbox and Grid, and responsive design.
web-development.html:
How CSS works

CSS applies rules to elements: a selector picks what to style, and declarations say how. h1 { color: navy; font-size: 2rem; }

When two rules conflict, the more specific one wins (an id beats a class, a class beats a tag). If they tie, whichever comes last wins. That is the whole "cascade".

The box model — the concept beginners trip over

Every element is a box with four layers, inside out: content → padding (space inside, within the background) → border → margin (space outside, pushing other elements away).

By default, width applies to the content only, so padding and border make the box wider than you asked. Fix it once, globally:

* { box-sizing: border-box; } — now width means the whole box. Every professional stylesheet starts with this.

Units

  • px — fixed. Fine for borders.
  • rem — relative to the root font size. Best for text and spacing; respects the user's settings.
  • % and vw/vh — relative to the parent or the screen. Good for layout.

Flexbox — laying things out in a line

Set display: flex on a container and its children line up in a row. Then justify-content spaces them along that row, align-items positions them across it, and gap puts space between them. Perfect for navigation bars, button rows and card contents.

Grid — laying things out in two dimensions

display: grid with grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(200px, 1fr)) gives you a product grid that reflows at any screen width without a single media query. Use Grid for page layout, Flexbox for the pieces inside it.

Responsive design

Start with the phone layout and add complexity for larger screens — mobile-first is easier than stripping a desktop design down. Add the viewport tag in your <head> or nothing will work:

<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

Then widen with media queries: @media (min-width: 768px) { … }

In Uganda most of your visitors are on a phone, often on mobile data. Test on a real phone, and keep images small.

web-development.title: JavaScript & Dynamic Pages
web-development.summary: Variables, functions, the DOM, events and talking to a server.
web-development.html:
What JavaScript adds

HTML gives structure, CSS gives appearance, JavaScript gives behaviour — menus that open, forms that validate before sending, content that loads without a page refresh.

The basics

  • Variables — let for values that change, const for values that don't. Avoid var.
  • Types — string, number, boolean, array, object, null, undefined.
  • Functions — reusable blocks: function total(a, b) { return a + b; }
  • Conditions — if / else, and === for comparison (never ==, which converts types and surprises you).
  • Loops — for, while, and array methods like map, filter, forEach.

The DOM

The browser turns your HTML into a tree of objects — the DOM. JavaScript changes the page by changing that tree:

  • document.querySelector('.price') — find an element.
  • el.textContent = 'UGX 500,000' — change its text.
  • el.classList.add('hidden') — change its styling.

Events

Events are things that happen: a click, a key press, a form submit. You respond with a listener:

button.addEventListener('click', () => { menu.classList.toggle('open'); });

Talking to a server

fetch() requests data without reloading the page. Because it takes time, it is asynchronous — you wait for it with async/await:

const res = await fetch('/api/products'); const data = await res.json();

Always handle failure. Phone networks drop constantly, and a site that freezes on a failed request looks broken.

Validation happens twice

Check the form in the browser so the user gets instant feedback — then check it again on the server. Anyone can bypass your JavaScript. Client-side validation is a convenience; server-side validation is the actual security.

Never trust input from a browser. That single sentence prevents most web vulnerabilities you will meet.

python-programming.title: Programming Foundations with Python
python-programming.summary: What a program is, how Python runs, variables, types and input.
python-programming.html:
What a program really is

A program is a list of instructions a computer follows exactly, in order. The computer has no judgement — it does precisely what you wrote, which is why most bugs are the program doing exactly what you said rather than what you meant.

Why Python

Python reads almost like English, so you spend your effort on the problem instead of the punctuation. It is used for websites, data analysis, automation, and AI — one language that takes you a long way.

Running Python

Two ways: the interactive shell (type a line, see the result — perfect for testing an idea) and a script file ending in .py that runs top to bottom. Real work lives in files.

Variables

A variable is a labelled box holding a value: price = 650000. Python works out the type itself. Names should say what they hold — total_price, not tp.

The core data types

  • int — whole numbers: 25
  • float — decimals: 19.99
  • str — text in quotes: "Kampala"
  • bool — True or False

Working with text

Join text with f-strings — the modern, readable way:

name = "Sarah"
print(f"Hello {name}, your total is UGX {total:,}")

Getting input

age = input("Your age: ") always returns text, even when the user types digits. Convert before doing maths: age = int(age). Forgetting this is the single most common beginner error.

Indentation is syntax in Python. Other languages use braces; Python uses four spaces. Get it wrong and the program will not run — which forces everyone to write readable code.

python-programming.title: Control Flow, Lists & Dictionaries
python-programming.summary: Decisions, loops, and the data structures you will use daily.
python-programming.html:
Making decisions

if runs a block only when a condition is true; elif checks another; else catches everything left:

if score >= 80:
    grade = "A"
elif score >= 60:
    grade = "B"
else:
    grade = "F"

Loops

  • for — repeat once per item: for item in cart:. Use when you know the collection.
  • while — repeat while something stays true. Use when you don't know how many rounds. Make sure the condition eventually becomes false, or the program hangs.

break leaves a loop early; continue skips to the next round.

Lists — ordered collections

prices = [650000, 900000, 1200000]

  • Counting starts at zero: prices[0] is the first item.
  • append() adds, remove() deletes, len() counts, sort() orders.
  • Negative indexes count from the end: prices[-1] is the last.

Dictionaries — labelled data

Where a list uses positions, a dictionary uses keys:

laptop = {"brand": "HP", "ram": "16GB", "price": 1900000}
print(laptop["brand"])

This is how almost all real data arrives — from a web API, a database row, a config file. Learn dictionaries well and the rest of programming opens up.

Choosing between them

Use a list when order matters and the items are the same kind of thing (all the prices). Use a dictionary when each value means something different (one laptop's brand, RAM and price).

python-programming.title: Functions, Files & Errors
python-programming.summary: Writing reusable code, saving data, and handling what goes wrong.
python-programming.html:
Functions

A function packages a job so you can reuse it:

def total_with_vat(amount, rate=0.18):
    return amount * (1 + rate)

Parameters are the inputs; return sends a value back. rate=0.18 is a default — callers can omit it.

Why functions matter

  • No repetition — fix a bug once, not in twelve places.
  • Testable — you can check one function in isolation.
  • Readable — a good name explains a block of logic at a glance.
One function, one job. If you struggle to name it, it is probably doing too much — split it.

Scope

Variables made inside a function exist only there. That is deliberate: it stops one part of a program quietly corrupting another.

Working with files

Use with, which closes the file for you even if something fails:

with open("sales.txt", "r") as f:
    lines = f.readlines()

Modes: "r" read, "w" write (erases the file first), "a" append. Confusing "w" with "a" has destroyed a lot of data.

Errors and exceptions

Programs meet the unexpected: a missing file, a user typing "abc" for their age, the network down. Handle it:

try:
    age = int(input("Age: "))
except ValueError:
    print("Please type a number.")

Catch the specific error you expect. A bare except: swallows every problem including your own bugs, and you end up debugging blind.

Modules

Python ships with a large standard library — math, datetime, random, json, csv. Import what you need: import datetime. Install extra packages with pip. Before writing something from scratch, check whether it already exists.

computer-networking.title: Networking Fundamentals
computer-networking.summary: What a network is, types, topologies and the OSI model.
computer-networking.html:
What a network is

A network is two or more devices connected so they can share data and resources — files, a printer, an internet line. Everything else in this course is detail on top of that idea.

Types by size

  • LAN (Local Area Network) — one building: an office, a school lab.
  • WAN (Wide Area Network) — across towns or countries. The internet is the largest WAN.
  • MAN — a city-wide network.
  • PAN — personal, a few metres: your phone and a Bluetooth speaker.

Topologies — how devices are arranged

  • Star — every device connects to a central switch. The standard today: one failed cable affects one device only.
  • Bus — all share one backbone cable. Cheap, obsolete; one break kills everything.
  • Ring — each connects to two neighbours.
  • Mesh — everything connects to everything. Very resilient, very expensive. Used between core sites.

The OSI model — seven layers

A map for understanding and fixing networks, from the wire up:

  1. Physical — cables, signals, radio.
  2. Data Link — MAC addresses, switches.
  3. Network — IP addresses, routers.
  4. Transport — TCP and UDP.
  5. Session — keeping conversations open.
  6. Presentation — encryption, formats.
  7. Application — what the user sees: HTTP, email.
Troubleshoot from layer 1 upward. Before blaming the server, check the cable is in. Most "network faults" are physical.

TCP vs UDP

TCP confirms delivery and re-sends what got lost — used for web pages, email, file transfer. UDP just fires packets without checking — used for voice and video calls, where a late packet is worse than a missing one.

computer-networking.title: IP Addressing & Subnetting
computer-networking.summary: Addresses, classes, private ranges, DHCP, DNS and NAT.
computer-networking.html:
IP addresses

An IP address identifies a device on a network. IPv4 looks like 192.168.1.10 — four numbers, each 0–255. Every address has two parts: the network portion (which network) and the host portion (which device on it).

The subnet mask

The mask says where that split falls. With 255.255.255.0 (written /24), the first three numbers are the network and the last identifies the device — so 192.168.1.x gives you 254 usable addresses.

Private vs public

Private ranges are reserved for internal networks and are never routed on the internet:

  • 10.0.0.0 – 10.255.255.255
  • 172.16.0.0 – 172.31.255.255
  • 192.168.0.0 – 192.168.255.255

Your whole office shares one public IP from the ISP. NAT on the router translates between the private addresses inside and that single public address outside.

Why subnet at all

  • Performance — smaller broadcast domains mean less noise.
  • Security — keep guest Wi-Fi off the accounts network.
  • Order — a predictable address plan makes faults obvious.

DHCP

DHCP hands out addresses automatically as devices join. Without it you would configure every phone by hand. Give servers, printers and network gear static addresses (or DHCP reservations) so they never move.

DNS

DNS translates names to addresses. "The internet is down" very often means DNS is down — everything still routes, but nothing resolves. Test it: if ping 8.8.8.8 works but ping google.com fails, it is DNS.

IPv6

IPv4 has run out of addresses. IPv6 uses much longer addresses like 2001:0db8:85a3::8a2e:0370:7334 — enough for every device for the foreseeable future. Most networks now run both.

computer-networking.title: Devices, Cabling & Troubleshooting
computer-networking.summary: Switches, routers, Wi-Fi, cable standards and a method for finding faults.
computer-networking.html:
The devices and what each one does

  • Switch — connects devices inside a LAN and sends each frame only to its destination (layer 2, by MAC address).
  • Router — joins different networks and chooses paths between them (layer 3, by IP). Your "internet box" is usually a router, switch, Wi-Fi access point and modem in one case.
  • Access point — provides Wi-Fi.
  • Firewall — filters traffic by rules; your first line of defence.
  • Hub — obsolete: repeats every frame to every port, wasting bandwidth.

Cabling

Cat5e handles gigabit and is fine for most offices; Cat6 is better for longer or noisier runs. The hard limit is 100 metres per run — beyond that, add a switch. Terminate to T568B consistently at both ends. A "straight-through" cable connects unlike devices; modern gear auto-senses, so crossover cables are rarely needed.

Wi-Fi in practice

  • 2.4 GHz — travels further, passes through walls, slower and congested.
  • 5 GHz — much faster, shorter range.
  • Use WPA2 or WPA3; never WEP.
  • Change the router's default admin password — attackers know the defaults.
  • Give visitors a separate guest network.

A method for troubleshooting

  1. Define the problem — one device or everyone? Since when? What changed?
  2. Check the physical layer — cables, link lights, power.
  3. Work up the layers — does it have an IP? Can it reach the gateway? The internet? By name?
  4. Test one change at a time, or you will never know what fixed it.
  5. Document it — the same fault returns.

The commands worth memorising

  • ipconfig /all — your address, gateway and DNS.
  • ping — is it reachable?
  • tracert — where along the path does it stop?
  • nslookup — is DNS resolving?
  • netstat -an — what connections are open?
An address starting 169.254 means DHCP failed — the device gave up and assigned itself one. Check the cable, then the DHCP server.

data-analysis-excel.title: The analysis workflow & clean data
data-analysis-excel.summary: How a real analysis job runs, and how to get messy data into shape first.
data-analysis-excel.html:
What data analysis actually is

Analysis is not "making charts". It is answering a question with evidence. Every job you will be given follows the same five steps:

  • Ask — what exactly is the question? "Are we losing money?" is not answerable. "Which branch had the lowest margin last quarter?" is.
  • Get — collect the data: an export from a system, a sales book, a bank statement.
  • Clean — fix what is wrong before you calculate anything.
  • Analyse — functions, PivotTables, comparisons.
  • Present — say what you found in one sentence, then show it.

Most beginners rush to step four. Professionals spend most of their time on step three, because a calculation on dirty data is worse than no calculation — it looks authoritative and is wrong.

Setting the file up properly

Excel works best when your data is a simple rectangle: one header row, then one record per row, no blank rows, no merged cells, no totals inside the data.

  • One column = one kind of thing. Never put "Kampala - 250,000" in a single cell. Split it into Branch and Amount.
  • No merged cells anywhere in the data. Merging breaks sorting, filtering and PivotTables.
  • Keep totals outside the data block, or better, let a PivotTable produce them.
  • Name your sheets. "Sheet1" tells the next person nothing.

Cleaning messy data

These are the problems you will meet on almost every real file:

  • Numbers stored as text — they sit on the left of the cell and refuse to sum. Fix with Data › Text to Columns › Finish, or multiply by 1.
  • Stray spaces — "Kampala " and "Kampala" are two different branches to Excel. Use =TRIM(A2).
  • Inconsistent case — use =PROPER(A2) or =UPPER(A2) to standardise.
  • Duplicates — Data › Remove Duplicates. Always copy the sheet first, so you can check how many rows disappeared.
  • Dates that are not dates — if they will not sort chronologically, they are text. Re-enter or use Text to Columns with the Date option.

Practice

Take any sales export you can find. Before calculating anything, answer: how many rows? Any duplicates? Any blanks? Do the totals in the file match a fresh SUM? Write the answers down. That habit alone will put you ahead of most people who list Excel on a CV.

data-analysis-excel.title: The functions that do the real work
data-analysis-excel.summary: IF, SUMIF, COUNTIF and the lookup family — with the traps that catch beginners.
data-analysis-excel.html:
IF — asking a question of every row

=IF(test, value_if_true, value_if_false). It reads exactly like English.

=IF(B2>1000000, "Large", "Normal") labels every sale over a million shillings.

You can nest them, but stop at three levels — beyond that use IFS or a lookup table, because nested IFs become impossible to check.

SUMIF and COUNTIF — totals with a condition

  • =SUMIF(range, criteria, sum_range) — "add up the amounts where the branch is Kampala": =SUMIF(A:A, "Kampala", C:C)
  • =COUNTIF(range, criteria) — "how many sales over 500,000?": =COUNTIF(C:C, ">500000")
  • SUMIFS and COUNTIFS take several conditions. Note the argument order flips: the sum range comes first in SUMIFS.

Write criteria with the operator inside quotes: ">500000", not >500000.

Lookups — pulling data from another table

This is the single most valuable Excel skill in an office. You have a sales sheet with product codes, and a price list on another sheet. A lookup joins them.

  • VLOOKUP(value, table, column_number, FALSE) — the old standard. The FALSE is not optional: leave it out and Excel guesses approximately, returning confidently wrong answers.
  • VLOOKUP can only look right from the key column, and breaks if someone inserts a column.
  • XLOOKUP(value, lookup_array, return_array) — newer, simpler, looks in any direction, and takes an "if not found" argument. Use it where your Excel has it.
  • INDEX/MATCH — =INDEX(C:C, MATCH(A2, B:B, 0)). Works everywhere, survives inserted columns. Learn it as your fallback.

When a lookup returns #N/A

It means "not found", and 90% of the time the cause is one of these: trailing spaces (TRIM both sides), one side stored as text and the other as a number, or you forgot the FALSE. Wrap it for presentation once you have checked it is genuine: =IFERROR(VLOOKUP(...), "Not found"). Never wrap in IFERROR before you understand why it failed — you will hide a real problem.

data-analysis-excel.title: Tables, PivotTables & Power Query
data-analysis-excel.summary: Turning thousands of rows into an answer in under a minute.
data-analysis-excel.html:
Format as Table first

Select your data and press Ctrl + T. A real Excel Table gives you filter buttons, banded rows, and most importantly a name and automatic expansion: add a row at the bottom and every formula, chart and PivotTable built on it includes the new row without being touched.

Rename it from "Table1" to something meaningful in Table Design. Formulas then read =SUM(Sales[Amount]) instead of =SUM(C2:C4000), which anyone can understand a year later.

PivotTables

A PivotTable summarises thousands of rows by dragging fields. Insert › PivotTable, then:

  • Rows — what you want to break the numbers down by (Branch, Product, Month).
  • Values — what you want to measure (Amount). Click it to switch between Sum, Count and Average.
  • Columns — a second breakdown across the top. Use sparingly; two breakdowns is usually enough to read.
  • Filters — or better, add a Slicer (PivotTable Analyze › Insert Slicer) for buttons anyone can click.

Right-click a value › Show Values As › % of Grand Total turns shillings into shares, which is usually the more useful answer.

A PivotTable does not update on its own. Right-click › Refresh after the source changes. Forgetting this is the most common cause of a report that quietly goes stale.

Power Query — for the job you do every month

Data › Get Data. Power Query records your cleaning steps and replays them on next month's file with one click. If you find yourself doing the same Text-to-Columns and Remove-Duplicates every month, that is exactly what it is for.

Typical use: load the raw export, remove the top junk rows, promote headers, set data types, trim text, then Close & Load. Next month, drop in the new file and press Refresh.

data-analysis-excel.title: Charts and conditional formatting that mean something
data-analysis-excel.summary: Choosing the right chart, and making numbers readable at a glance.
data-analysis-excel.html:
Pick the chart for the question

  • Comparing categories (sales by branch) → bar chart. Horizontal bars if the labels are long.
  • Change over time (monthly revenue) → line chart.
  • Parts of a whole → a bar chart, almost always. Pie charts are hard to read beyond three slices and impossible to compare between charts.
  • Relationship between two numbers → scatter.

Never use 3D. It distorts the very thing the reader is trying to judge.

Making a chart readable

  • Give it a title that states the finding, not the data: "Nakawa branch is down 18%" beats "Sales by branch".
  • Sort bars largest to smallest unless the order means something (like months).
  • Delete gridlines, the legend where there is one series, and any axis nobody reads.
  • Label directly on the bars where you can — a reader should not have to trace across to an axis.

Conditional formatting

Home › Conditional Formatting. Used well it lets someone read a table without reading the numbers.

  • Data bars — an in-cell bar chart. Best single option for a column of amounts.
  • Colour scales — good for spotting hot and cold areas across a grid.
  • Highlight cell rules — flag anything below target in red.
  • Top/Bottom rules — the top 10 customers, instantly.

Use one rule per table, two at most. When everything is coloured, nothing stands out — which defeats the purpose.

Number formatting
