Shillings should read as shillings. Select the column, Ctrl + 1, Number, tick Use 1000 Separator, 0 decimal places. For big figures use a custom format of #,##0,," M" to show 4,310,000 as "4 M" — easier to compare at a glance.

data-analysis-excel.title: Building a dashboard & presenting findings
data-analysis-excel.summary: Putting it together into one page a manager can use, and saying what it means.
data-analysis-excel.html:
What a dashboard is for

A dashboard answers the same few questions every week without anybody rebuilding it. It is one screen, no scrolling, and it updates by pressing Refresh.

Build it in layers

  1. Data sheet — the raw table, untouched. Nobody reads this.
  2. Working sheet — PivotTables and calculations. Hidden from the reader.
  3. Dashboard sheet — charts and big numbers only, linked to the working sheet.

Keeping these separate is what makes a dashboard survive contact with new data. Mixing raw data and presentation on one sheet is why most spreadsheets break.

Laying it out

  • Top-left is the most valuable space — put the headline number there (total revenue, this month).
  • Three to five KPI tiles across the top: the number, and how it compares to last month.
  • Two or three charts below, no more.
  • One set of Slicers controlling everything. Connect a slicer to several PivotTables via Report Connections.
  • Turn off gridlines (View › Gridlines) — it stops looking like a spreadsheet and starts looking like a report.

Presenting the findings

The chart is not the finding. Before you send anything, write one sentence: what happened, by how much, and what you think should be done.

"Nakawa revenue fell 18% (UGX 4.2M) in Q3, driven entirely by accessories. Stock records show we were out of chargers for 11 days. Recommend a reorder point." That is analysis. A chart with no sentence is just decoration.

Be honest about limits. If two weeks of data were missing, say so. Your credibility is worth more than a tidy conclusion.

quickbooks-accounting.title: Bookkeeping basics every owner needs
quickbooks-accounting.summary: The few accounting ideas that make QuickBooks make sense.
quickbooks-accounting.html:
Why bookkeeping exists

A business has to answer three questions at any moment: what do we own, what do we owe, and did we make a profit? Bookkeeping is the record that answers them. QuickBooks is just a tool for keeping that record; it will not save you if you do not understand what it is recording.

Money in is not profit

This is the single most expensive misunderstanding in small business. Cash arriving is not the same as money earned, and cash leaving is not the same as a cost.

  • A customer pays you UGX 5,000,000 deposit for goods you have not delivered. That is cash in, but not yet revenue — you owe them goods.
  • You buy a laptop for the office for UGX 3,000,000. That is cash out, but not a cost this month — it is an asset that wears out over years.

Businesses with full bank accounts go under because they mistake cash for profit. Keep the two ideas separate from day one.

The five types of account

  • Assets — what you own: cash, bank, stock, equipment, money customers owe you.
  • Liabilities — what you owe: suppliers, loans, unpaid VAT.
  • Equity — the owner's share: what you put in, plus profits kept in.
  • Income — what you earned from trading.
  • Expenses — what it cost to earn it: rent, salaries, data, transport.

Every transaction touches at least two of these. Sell a laptop for cash: Assets go up (cash) and Income goes up. Pay rent: Assets go down (cash) and Expenses go up. That is double-entry, and QuickBooks does it for you once the accounts are set up correctly.

The one rule that matters most

Never mix personal and business money. A separate business account and a separate mobile money line. Every hour you save now by mixing them costs a day later trying to separate them — and makes your figures meaningless in between.

quickbooks-accounting.title: Setting up your company & chart of accounts
quickbooks-accounting.summary: Getting the foundations right, because fixing them later is painful.
quickbooks-accounting.html:
Company setup

When you create the company file, QuickBooks asks for the essentials. Take them seriously — several cannot be changed easily later.

  • Company name and address — exactly as it appears on your trading licence; this prints on every invoice.
  • Currency — UGX as your home currency. If you buy in USD, enable multi-currency now; switching later is a rebuild.
  • Financial year start — usually July in Uganda to match the government year, but January is fine if that is how you report.
  • TIN — put it in the company settings so it prints on invoices. URA-compliant invoices need it.
  • Accounting method — Accrual records the sale when you invoice; Cash records it when paid. Accrual gives a truer picture; small traders often start on Cash.

The chart of accounts

This is the list of buckets every shilling falls into. QuickBooks gives you a default list; your job is to trim it to your business.

Keep it short. A small business needs perhaps 30 accounts, not 200. If you cannot decide which of two accounts a cost belongs in, you have one account too many — merge them.

A workable set for a Kampala retail or services business:

  • Income: Sales — Goods, Sales — Services, Other income.
  • Cost of sales: Purchases, Freight & clearing.
  • Expenses: Rent, Salaries & wages, NSSF, Electricity, Internet & airtime, Transport & fuel, Repairs, Bank charges, Licences & permits, Marketing, Stationery.
  • Assets: Cash on hand, Bank — [name], Mobile money, Accounts receivable, Stock, Equipment.
  • Liabilities: Accounts payable, VAT payable, Loans.

Opening balances

Pick a start date — the first day of a month. Enter what you owned and owed on that date: bank balance, cash, stock value, unpaid customer invoices, unpaid supplier bills. Get this right and everything afterwards reconciles. Get it wrong and every report is off by the same amount forever.

quickbooks-accounting.title: Sales, invoices, expenses & bills
quickbooks-accounting.summary: The daily work: recording what you sell and what you spend.
quickbooks-accounting.html:
Customers and the sales cycle

QuickBooks separates a promise to pay from the payment itself, and it matters:

  • Invoice — you delivered, they will pay later. Creates a receivable.
  • Sales receipt — they paid on the spot. No receivable.
  • Receive payment — matches money received against an existing invoice.
  • Estimate / quote — not a sale at all; no accounting effect until converted.

The common mistake is recording a bank deposit as new income when it was payment of an invoice already recorded. That doubles your revenue and your tax. Always use Receive Payment against the invoice.

Writing a proper invoice

  • Unique sequential number — never reuse or skip.
  • Your TIN and the customer's, for VAT-registered trade.
  • Clear description, quantity, unit price, line total.
  • VAT shown separately where you are registered.
  • Payment terms and how to pay (bank, mobile money) written on it.

Expenses and bills

  • Expense — paid immediately (fuel, airtime, a taxi).
  • Bill — a supplier invoice to pay later. Creates a payable.
  • Pay bills — settles it. Again, do not record the payment as a fresh expense; that double-counts the cost.

Attach the photo of the receipt to the transaction. QuickBooks lets you attach an image, and a record with a receipt attached is worth far more in a URA audit than a line of text.

Discipline beats catching up

Twenty minutes daily is easier than a day at month-end, and the figures are usable all month instead of only after the scramble. Set a fixed time and keep it.

quickbooks-accounting.title: Bank reconciliation, VAT & payroll
quickbooks-accounting.summary: Proving your books are right, and the statutory bits you cannot skip.
quickbooks-accounting.html:
Bank reconciliation

Reconciling means proving your books agree with the bank. Do it monthly, without exception. It is the only routine check that catches a missed entry, a duplicate, or a theft.

  1. Get the statement for the period and its closing balance.
  2. Banking › Reconcile, enter the statement end date and closing balance.
  3. Tick every transaction that appears on the statement.
  4. The difference must reach zero.

When it will not balance, look for: an amount entered with digits transposed (a difference divisible by 9), a transaction entered twice, bank charges never recorded, or a payment dated in the wrong month. Never force it with an adjusting entry you do not understand — that hides the very error you are looking for.

VAT in Uganda

VAT is 18%. Registration is required once turnover passes the threshold set by URA, and voluntary below it. Check the current threshold with URA or your accountant — it changes.

  • Output VAT — what you charge customers.
  • Input VAT — what you paid suppliers, on valid VAT invoices.
  • You remit the difference. Input VAT without a proper invoice bearing the supplier's TIN cannot be claimed, so file them carefully.

Set VAT up in QuickBooks before your first invoice and apply the right code per line. Some items are zero-rated or exempt, and the two are not the same thing — ask your accountant which applies to your goods.

VAT collected is not your money. It sits in your account on URA's behalf. Businesses that spend it end up borrowing to pay the return.

Payroll basics

For each employee you handle PAYE (income tax, deducted from the employee), NSSF (currently 5% employee, 10% employer), and Local Service Tax where it applies. Deadlines matter more than amounts — penalties for late filing are avoidable and expensive.

Keep signed payslips. A payroll record without evidence the employee received it is weak in a dispute.

quickbooks-accounting.title: Reports, month-end & staying organised
quickbooks-accounting.summary: Reading your own numbers, and a routine that keeps them trustworthy.
quickbooks-accounting.html:
The three reports that matter

  • Profit & Loss — income less expenses over a period. Did we make money this month?
  • Balance Sheet — what we own and owe at a single date. Assets = Liabilities + Equity, always.
  • Cash Flow — where cash actually moved. Explains a profitable month with an empty account.

Reading a P&L properly

Do not read a single month alone. Set the comparison to the previous period or last year, and read the percentages:

  • Gross margin = (Sales − Cost of sales) ÷ Sales. If this slips, either you are buying dearer or discounting harder.
  • Expenses as a share of sales — rising costs against flat sales is the early warning most owners miss.
  • Anything that moved more than about 20% deserves an explanation before you accept it.

The month-end routine

  1. Enter every outstanding invoice and bill.
  2. Reconcile every bank, cash and mobile money account.
  3. Review Accounts Receivable — who owes you and for how long. Chase anything over 30 days that day.
  4. Review Accounts Payable — what falls due next month.
  5. Check stock on hand against the system, and investigate differences.
  6. Run and read the P&L and Balance Sheet.
  7. Close the books for the period so nobody edits history.

Records and backups

URA can ask you to support any figure. Keep invoices, receipts, bank statements and payroll records for the retention period your accountant advises. Attach scans in QuickBooks and keep the paper — phones are lost and cloud accounts are locked out.

If you use QuickBooks Desktop, back up weekly to somewhere that is not the same computer. QuickBooks Online backs itself up, but export a copy of your reports at year-end regardless. A business that cannot produce its own numbers cannot borrow, sell itself, or defend an assessment.

microsoft-365-teams.title: What Microsoft 365 is & OneDrive
microsoft-365-teams.summary: How the pieces fit together, and getting your files off the desktop.
microsoft-365-teams.html:
The idea

Microsoft 365 is the Office programs you know, plus the services that let a team use them together: files that live online, email, chat, meetings and shared notes. The change from old Office is not the programs — it is that your work stops living on one computer.

What that buys you: your files on any device, no more "final_v3_REAL.docx", two people editing one document at once, and a laptop theft that costs you a laptop instead of your business.

The main parts

  • OneDrive — your own file store. Think of it as My Documents, online.
  • SharePoint — the team's file store. Files that belong to the organisation, not a person.
  • Outlook — email and calendar.
  • Teams — chat, meetings, and a front door to the files above.
  • Word, Excel, PowerPoint — desktop and in the browser.
  • OneNote — shared notebooks.

OneDrive in practice

Install OneDrive and sign in, and a OneDrive folder appears in File Explorer. Anything you put there syncs. Work in it exactly as you always have.

  • Green tick — synced and on this device. Cloud icon — online only, downloads when opened. Arrows — syncing now.
  • Files On-Demand keeps everything visible without filling a small disk. Right-click › Always keep on this device for anything you need offline — do this before travelling.
  • Version history — right-click any file › Version history. You can recover yesterday's version after someone overwrites it. This alone justifies the move.
  • Recycle bin keeps deleted files for 30 days.

Personal vs team files

Rule of thumb: if the work would still matter after you left the organisation, it belongs in the team's SharePoint or a Teams channel, not your OneDrive. Files stuck in a departed employee's OneDrive are a common and avoidable problem.

microsoft-365-teams.title: Outlook: email and calendar that stay under control
microsoft-365-teams.summary: Handling mail without living in it, and running a diary people trust.
microsoft-365-teams.html:
Getting the inbox under control

The inbox is a list of things other people want. Treat each message once:

  • Under two minutes — do it now.
  • Longer — flag it, or drag it to the calendar to make time for it.
  • Someone else's — forward it and move on.
  • Reference — file it. One "Archive" folder is enough; search finds things faster than folders.

Turn off desktop notifications for mail. Nothing arriving by email needs a response within seconds, and the interruption costs more than it saves.

Rules, Focused Inbox and Sweep

  • Rules — file newsletters and system notices on arrival so they never reach the inbox.
  • Focused Inbox — splits likely-important from the rest. Correct it a few times and it learns.
  • Sweep — delete all mail from a sender, or keep only the latest.

Writing mail people actually act on

  • A subject line that states the point: "Invoice 2041 — approval needed by Friday".
  • The ask in the first sentence. Context after.
  • One topic per email. Two topics means half your request gets ignored.
  • To = must act. Cc = for information. Anyone in Cc should be able to ignore it safely.
  • Reply All only when everyone genuinely needs it.

The calendar

  • Invite people rather than emailing a time — invitations update when things move.
  • Use Scheduling Assistant to see when people are free instead of negotiating by mail.
  • Give every meeting an agenda in the invitation body. No agenda, no meeting.
  • Block your own focused time as an appointment, or it will be booked over.
  • Set working hours so colleagues in other time zones do not invite you at 9pm.

microsoft-365-teams.title: Teams: chat, channels and meetings
microsoft-365-teams.summary: Using Teams so it replaces email rather than adding to it.
microsoft-365-teams.html:
Chat vs channels

This is the distinction that decides whether Teams helps or becomes noise.

  • Chat — private, between people. Good for quick and personal things. Bad for anything the team will need later, because nobody else can find it.
  • Channels — inside a Team, open to its members, organised by topic. Good for work. A new person can scroll back and catch up.

Default to a channel. Use chat when it genuinely concerns only those people.

Setting up Teams and channels

  • One Team per real group — a department, a project, a branch. Not per task.
  • Channels per topic within it: General, Sales, Suppliers, Marketing.
  • Every channel has a Files tab — that is SharePoint. Files dropped there belong to the team automatically.
  • Pin key documents as tabs across the top so nobody hunts for the price list.

Posting so people respond

  • Use the subject line on important posts — it makes them scannable.
  • Reply inside a thread rather than starting a new post. Broken threads are the main reason channels become unreadable.
  • @name for someone you need, @channel sparingly, @team almost never.
  • Mark it Important only when it truly is, or the marker stops meaning anything.

Meetings

  • Schedule from the Teams calendar, or hit Meet now in a channel for something immediate.
  • Blur or replace your background if the room is busy.
  • Mute on join, always, on any call with more than three people.
  • Share screen — share the window, not the whole desktop, so your notifications stay private.
  • Record for anyone who could not attend; tell people first.
  • Live captions help enormously on a weak connection.

On limited data, turn off incoming video. Audio uses a fraction of what video does, and the meeting still works.

microsoft-365-teams.title: Working together on files, and sharing safely
microsoft-365-teams.summary: Co-editing, permissions and the mistakes that leak documents.
microsoft-365-teams.html:
Co-authoring

Open a Word, Excel or PowerPoint file stored in OneDrive or a Teams channel and several people can edit it at once. You see their cursors with their names. There is no "who has it open?" and no merging afterwards.

  • It saves continuously — there is no Save button to forget.
  • Version history (File › Info › Version History) restores any earlier state.
  • Comments with @name email that person the comment. Use them instead of a separate email about the document.
  • Track Changes still exists for formal review where every edit must be approved.

The browser versions do most of what the desktop does. Use desktop for heavy formatting, long documents and large spreadsheets.

Sharing — the part people get wrong

Press Share and read the box carefully before sending. The default may be broader than you think.

  • Anyone with the link — works for people outside, and works for anyone the link is forwarded to. Treat as public.
  • People in your organisation — safer default for internal work.
  • Specific people — the right choice for anything sensitive.

Then set whether they can edit or only view, add an expiry date for outside parties, and switch off Allow downloading when you want it read but not copied.

Good habits

  • Share a link, never an attachment. An attachment is a copy that immediately goes stale and cannot be withdrawn.
  • Review sharing periodically: Manage access on important files, and remove people who have moved on.
  • Never share payroll, contracts or ID documents with "Anyone with the link".
  • Turn on multi-factor authentication. A password alone is not enough for an account holding everything your business does.

microsoft-365-teams.title: OneNote, any device, and working faster
microsoft-365-teams.summary: Shared notes, phone and offline use, and the shortcuts worth learning.
microsoft-365-teams.html:
OneNote

A notebook that syncs, structured as Notebooks › Sections › Pages. Type anywhere on a page, paste images, tick checkboxes, record audio.

Where it earns its place in a business:

  • Meeting notes in a shared section, so decisions are not trapped in one person's book.
  • Procedures — how to process an order, how to close the shop. New staff read it instead of asking.
  • Client records — a page per client with history.
  • Tags — mark To Do, Important, Question, then use Find Tags to pull every open item across the notebook.

Add a OneNote section as a tab in a Teams channel and the team's notes live where the team already is.

Any device

  • Install Outlook, Teams, OneDrive and Office on your phone. Approving something from a boda is better than it waiting until Monday.
  • The Office Lens feature in the Office app photographs a document and straightens it into a PDF — a scanner in your pocket.
  • Mark files Always keep on this device before you travel or lose signal.
  • Outlook and OneNote work offline and sync when you reconnect. Compose replies on a bad connection; they will go.
  • On a public computer, use the browser and sign out afterwards. Never tick "stay signed in".

Shortcuts worth the effort

  • Ctrl + Shift + M — mute and unmute in a Teams meeting. The most useful one here.
  • Ctrl + E — search, in almost every Microsoft app.
  • Ctrl + Shift + V — paste without formatting. Saves endless tidying.
  • Ctrl + . in Teams — the full shortcut list.
  • In Outlook: Ctrl + R reply, Ctrl + Shift + R reply all, Ctrl + Shift + M new mail.

A weekly habit

Fifteen minutes on Friday: clear the inbox to zero or near it, look at next week's calendar and protect time for the work that matters, and check nothing important is sitting in a chat where the team cannot find it. The tools only help if something keeps them tidy.

video-editing.title: How editing works, and your kit
video-editing.summary: The craft behind the software, plus what you actually need to start.
video-editing.html:
Editing is decisions, not software

An editor decides three things over and over: what to show, for how long, and what comes next. CapCut and Premiere Pro are just ways of recording those decisions. Someone who understands pacing produces better work on a phone than someone who knows every button and has no judgement.

The vocabulary

  • Clip — one piece of footage. Timeline — where clips are arranged in order.
  • Cut — an instant change from one clip to another. Your default; use it 90% of the time.
  • B-roll — supporting footage laid over the main audio. It is what makes a talking-head watchable.
  • J-cut / L-cut — the audio of the next shot starts before its picture, or continues after. The single trick that makes editing feel professional.
  • Frame rate — 24fps is cinematic, 30fps standard, 60fps smooth and good for slow motion.
  • Resolution — 1080p is enough for almost everything. 4K only if you need to crop or the client demands it; it eats storage and battery.

Kit that matters, in order

  1. Sound — audiences forgive rough pictures and abandon bad audio instantly. A cheap lapel mic beats a better camera.
  2. Light — a window, or one LED panel. Never light from behind.
  3. Stability — a tripod, or brace against a wall.
  4. Camera — last. A recent phone is genuinely enough.

Before you shoot

Clean the lens. Set resolution and frame rate deliberately. Record 3 seconds before and after each take — it gives you room to cut. Shoot more B-roll than you think you need; you will want it and cannot invent it later.

Organise as you go: one folder per project, subfolders for Footage, Audio, Music, Exports. Editors lose more time to hunting for files than to editing.

video-editing.title: CapCut: cutting, pacing, text and sound
video-editing.summary: Getting a finished, watchable video out of the free tool on your phone or PC.
video-editing.html:
Getting started

CapCut is free, runs on Android, iPhone and PC, and does most of what a paid editor does. Import your clips, and they land on the timeline in order.

  • Split — position the playhead, tap Split. This is the whole job, repeated.
  • Trim — drag a clip's edge inward.
  • Reorder — hold and drag.
  • Speed — 1.5× a slow section rather than cutting it entirely.

Pacing

Cut on the end of a thought, not the end of a sentence. Remove every "um", every pause longer than about half a second, and every moment where nothing happens. Most first edits improve by cutting a third of their length.

Watch it back at full speed without touching anything. Wherever your attention drifts, that is where the audience leaves. Cut there.

Transitions

Use a plain cut almost always. A transition should mean something — a change of time or place. Spin, glitch and zoom transitions look amateurish within a week of using them. If you want one effect, use a short cross dissolve for a time passing.

Text and captions

  • Auto captions — CapCut generates them, then you correct the errors. Always correct them; auto captions mangle names and local words.
  • Most people watch without sound. Captions are not optional for social video.
  • Keep text large, high contrast, and away from the edges where interfaces cover it.
  • Two lines maximum on screen at once.

Audio

  • Voice around −6 dB, music around −20 dB underneath it. If you strain to hear the words, the music is too loud.
  • Fade music in and out; never let it stop dead.
  • Use royalty-free music, or your video gets muted or claimed on YouTube and Facebook.
  • Duck the music under speech — CapCut can do it automatically.

video-editing.title: Colour, and moving to Premiere Pro
video-editing.summary: Making footage look consistent, and what a professional timeline gives you.
video-editing.html:
Correction before grading

Two different jobs, in this order:

  1. Correction — make it look right. Fix exposure, white balance and contrast so white objects look white.
  2. Grading — make it look intentional. Warm for friendly, cool for corporate, desaturated for serious.

Correct every clip first so they match each other. Nothing marks amateur work like shots that jump between blue and orange within one sequence.

The controls that matter

  • White balance / temperature — fix indoor footage that has gone orange under bulbs.
  • Exposure — overall brightness. Recover shadows before touching exposure; lifting exposure blows out highlights permanently.
  • Contrast — small amounts. Heavy contrast crushes detail in darker skin tones especially.
  • Saturation — less than you want. Over-saturated skin looks unwell.

Grade on a screen you know, at normal brightness. A video graded on a phone at full brightness looks dark everywhere else.

Premiere Pro

The step up is not better effects — it is organisation and control on longer projects.

  • Project panel — bins for Footage, Audio, Music, Graphics. Discipline here saves hours later.
  • Source and Program monitors — review a clip and set In/Out points before it touches the timeline. Much faster than trimming afterwards.
  • Multiple video and audio tracks — V1 interview, V2 B-roll, A1 voice, A2 music.
  • Keyboard editing — I and O for in and out, Ctrl+K to cut, Q and W to trim to the playhead. Learn these five and you double your speed.
  • Adjustment layers — one grade applied to everything below it.
  • Proxies — edit smoothly with low-resolution copies, export from the originals. Essential on a modest laptop with 4K footage.

Save often, and enable auto-save. Premiere crashes.

video-editing.title: Exporting and a promo video project
video-editing.summary: Right settings per platform, and a complete job from brief to delivery.
video-editing.html:
Export settings

Use H.264 / MP4 for everything unless a client specifies otherwise. What changes per platform is shape and length.

  • YouTube — 1920×1080, 16:9 landscape, any length.
  • TikTok / Reels / Shorts — 1080×1920, 9:16 vertical, under 60 seconds.
  • WhatsApp — WhatsApp compresses hard. Export smaller (720p) and keep it under about 16MB, or it arrives unwatchable.
  • Facebook — 1080p, and square (1:1) often performs better in feed than landscape.

Export once per shape from the original edit. Never re-encode an already exported file — quality drops each time.

Name the file so the client can find it: ClientName_PromoV2_1080p.mp4, not final_final.mp4.

The promo video project

Brief: a 45-second promo for a Kampala business, for WhatsApp and Instagram.

  1. Plan — one sentence: what should a viewer do after watching? Everything serves that.
  2. Shot list — write it before shooting. Exterior, the product, hands using it, a customer, the owner speaking, contact details.
  3. Shoot — each shot twice, steady, 5 seconds each minimum. Record the owner's line several times.
  4. Assemble — lay the spoken audio first, then cover it with B-roll.
  5. Structure — hook in the first 3 seconds (the problem), the offer, proof, then the call to action with phone number on screen for a full 5 seconds.
  6. Polish — captions, music underneath, colour match, logo at the end.
  7. Export — one vertical, one square.

Working with clients

Agree in writing: how many rounds of revision, what the fee covers, and who owns the footage. Deliver on time and name the files properly. Most repeat business in this trade comes from being easy to work with, not from the fanciest edit.

photography-editing.title: Your camera, and composition
photography-editing.summary: Understanding the tool in your hand, and where to put things in the frame.
photography-editing.html:
The phone is a real camera

A recent phone takes photographs good enough to sell products, document events and build a portfolio. What it does not do is decide where to stand — and that decision matters more than the sensor.

  • Clean the lens. Pocket grease is the single biggest cause of soft, hazy phone photos.
  • Shoot at the highest resolution and turn on the grid in settings.
  • Avoid digital zoom — it crops and degrades. Walk closer.
  • Tap to focus, then slide to adjust exposure before shooting.
  • Shoot RAW if your phone offers it and you intend to edit. Far more recoverable detail; larger files.

Composition

  • Rule of thirds — place your subject on a grid line or intersection, not dead centre. Put a person's eyes on the upper line.
  • Leading lines — roads, fences and shadows that draw the eye to the subject.
  • Framing — shoot through a doorway or branches to add depth.
  • Fill the frame — get closer. Most weak photographs are simply too far away.
  • Negative space — deliberate emptiness makes a subject feel important, and leaves room for text on a poster.
  • Check the background before you press. A pole growing out of someone's head is the classic beginner's photo, and it cannot be fixed later.

Angle

Eye level is neutral. Lower makes a subject imposing. Higher makes it smaller, and is usually unflattering for portraits. For products, shoot at the height the product would sit on a shelf.

Move your feet before you touch a setting. Three steps left often fixes what no editing can.

photography-editing.title: Light and exposure
photography-editing.summary: The exposure triangle, and how to use the light you actually have.
photography-editing.html:
Light is the whole craft

"Photography" means drawing with light. Good light on an ordinary subject beats bad light on a beautiful one.

  • Soft light — cloudy day, open shade, near a window. Gentle shadows, flattering. Your default.
  • Hard light — midday sun. Harsh shadows, squinting. Avoid, or move into shade.
  • Golden hour — the hour after sunrise and before sunset. Warm, low, beautiful. Plan around it.
  • Backlight — light behind the subject. Either expose for the face and blow the background, or use it deliberately for a silhouette.

Indoors in Kampala, the best free studio is a large window with the subject facing it and you between them and the glass.

The exposure triangle

  • Aperture (f-number) — how wide the lens opens. f/1.8 lets in lots of light and blurs the background; f/8 keeps everything sharp. Low number = blurry background.
  • Shutter speed — how long the sensor is exposed. 1/500 freezes motion; 1/30 blurs it. Handheld, stay above roughly 1/60 or your hands will show.
  • ISO — sensitivity. 100 is clean; 3200 is noisy. Keep it as low as the light allows.

They trade against each other. Darker room: open the aperture, then slow the shutter, and raise ISO only as a last resort.

Practical settings

  • Portrait — f/1.8–f/2.8, 1/125, ISO as low as possible.
  • Product — f/8 for full sharpness, on a tripod, any shutter speed.
  • Event indoors — f/2.8, 1/125, ISO up to 1600. Accept some noise; blur cannot be fixed, noise partly can.

Check the histogram, not the screen. Bunched against the right edge means blown highlights that are gone for good. Slightly under-exposed is recoverable; over-exposed often is not.

photography-editing.title: Portraits and product photography
photography-editing.summary: Two paid jobs: photographing people, and photographing things that must sell.
photography-editing.html:
Portraits

  • Focus on the eyes. A sharp eye carries a portrait; everything else can be soft.
  • Shoot slightly above eye level and have them lean in slightly — it flattens the jaw and looks natural.
  • Soft light from the side gives shape. Flat frontal light is safe but lifeless.
  • Talk to the person. Genuine expressions come from conversation, not from "smile". Keep shooting between poses — the best frame is usually just after they relax.
  • For darker skin tones, expose for the skin, not the background, and avoid heavy contrast which crushes detail. Slightly warm light is flattering.

Take more frames than feels necessary. Blinks and half-expressions are invisible until you review.

Product photography for business

This is where the money is for most photographers in Uganda — every shop needs images that sell.

  • Clean background — white card or plain wall. Consistency across a catalogue matters more than creativity.
  • Soft, even light — a window plus a white card opposite to bounce light back into the shadows.
  • Tripod and f/8 — the whole product sharp, front to back.
  • Several angles — front, three-quarter, back, detail, and one in use. Buyers who cannot see it from every side do not buy.
  • Scale — one shot with a hand or a familiar object so size is obvious.
  • Consistency — same distance, same light, same background for every item. A catalogue where each photo differs looks untrustworthy.

Charging for it

Price per shoot or per product, not per hour — clients understand deliverables. Agree the number of final edited images, the turnaround, and usage rights up front, in a message you can both refer back to.

photography-editing.title: Editing: Snapseed, Lightroom and retouching
photography-editing.summary: Finishing photographs on phone and desktop, without overdoing it.
photography-editing.html:
Snapseed on the phone

Free, powerful, and enough for most work. A reliable order:

  1. Crop and straighten first — a tilted horizon undermines everything else.
  2. Tune Image — Brightness, Contrast, Saturation, Ambiance, Highlights, Shadows. Small moves.
  3. Selective — place a point on the subject and brighten just that area. The single most useful tool in Snapseed.
  4. Healing — remove a bin, a wire, a blemish.
  5. Details — a little Structure and Sharpening, last.

Snapseed edits non-destructively — tap the stack icon to go back and change any earlier step.

Lightroom

For volume and consistency. The order that works:

  • White balance — get whites white with the eyedropper.
  • Exposure, then Highlights down and Shadows up to recover detail at both ends.
  • Whites and Blacks — set the true white and black points for punch.
  • Clarity and Texture — gently. Clarity on skin looks harsh.
  • HSL — adjust individual colours. Pulling down orange saturation slightly evens out skin.

Copy and paste settings across a whole shoot, or save a preset. This is how a hundred photos get a consistent look in minutes — the real reason to use Lightroom.

Retouching, honestly

  • Remove temporary things — a spot, a stray hair, a plastic bag. Keep what makes the person themselves.
  • Never reshape bodies or faces without being asked. It is a real harm dressed up as a favour.
  • Skin should keep texture. Smoothed-to-plastic skin reads as fake and dates badly.
  • For products, removing dust and background marks is fine; changing the colour of the item is dishonest and gets you returns.

Exporting

  • Web / social — JPEG, 2048px on the long edge, quality 80, sRGB.
  • Client print — full resolution JPEG at quality 100.
  • Archive — keep the original RAW files. You cannot re-edit a JPEG later.

Back up to two places. A photographer who loses a client's shoot does not get a second job.

autocad.title: The interface, and drawing with precision
autocad.summary: Finding your way around, and the habit that separates CAD from sketching.
autocad.html:
The screen

  • Ribbon — tools grouped in tabs across the top.
  • Command line — the most important part of AutoCAD. Every action reports here and asks for what it needs next. Read it constantly. Beginners who ignore the command line stay stuck.
  • Drawing area — model space, where you draw at full size.
  • Status bar — the toggles: Snap, Grid, Ortho, Polar, Object Snap.

You can type every command. L for Line, C Circle, M Move, CO Copy, TR Trim, O Offset. Typing is faster than hunting the ribbon, and it is how experienced drafters work.

Esc cancels anything. When lost, press it twice and start again.

Navigation

Scroll wheel zooms, hold the wheel to pan, double-click the wheel for Zoom Extents — which brings everything back on screen when you have lost your drawing.

Draw full size, always

This is the rule people break first and regret. A 4-metre wall is drawn 4000 units long, not scaled down. Scaling happens only when printing. Set your units at the start: UNITS command, Decimal, and work in millimetres for building work.

Precision

CAD is not sketching. Never place a point by eye.

  • Absolute coordinates — 100,50 is an exact position.
  • Relative — @200,0 means 200 to the right of the last point. Your everyday tool.
  • Polar — @1500<90 means 1500 units at 90 degrees.
  • Direct distance — point the mouse in a direction, type 3000, press Enter. Fastest method with Ortho on.
  • Ortho (F8) — locks to horizontal and vertical.
  • Object Snap (F3) — snaps to endpoints, midpoints, centres, intersections. Turn on Endpoint, Midpoint, Centre, Intersection and Perpendicular, and leave the rest off or it fights you.

A drawing that looks right but is 3mm out is worthless — it will not dimension correctly and cannot be built from.

autocad.title: Modifying, layers and annotation
autocad.summary: The commands you will use all day, and organising a drawing others can read.
autocad.html:
Modify commands

  • MOVE (M) and COPY (CO) — select, Enter, pick a base point, pick the destination. Always pick a meaningful base point like a corner.
  • OFFSET (O) — parallel copy at a set distance. How wall thicknesses are drawn.
  • TRIM (TR) and EXTEND (EX) — cut back to, or stretch out to, another object. In recent versions just start Trim and click what you want gone.
  • FILLET (F) — round a corner; set radius 0 and it makes two lines meet cleanly instead. Used constantly for tidying.
  • MIRROR (MI) — symmetry. Draw half, mirror it.
  • ARRAY (AR) — many copies in a grid or circle. Columns, parking bays, bolt holes.
  • STRETCH (S) — move part of an object while staying connected. Select with a crossing window (right to left) or it will not work.

Selection: left-to-right selects only what is fully enclosed; right-to-left selects anything touched. This catches everyone at first.

Layers

Layers are how a drawing stays readable. Everything of one kind goes on its own layer, with its own colour and line type.

  • A typical set: Walls, Doors, Windows, Dimensions, Text, Furniture, Electrical, Hatch, Centre lines.
  • Colour drives lineweight when plotting — walls heavy, dimensions light.
  • Freeze a layer to hide it and speed up the drawing; Lock to see but not edit it.
  • Layer 0 is reserved for making blocks. Do not draw on it.

Set the layer before drawing, not after. Sorting out a drawing where everything is on one layer takes longer than drawing it again.

Dimensions and text

  • Create a dimension style once (DIMSTYLE) with text height and arrow size suited to your plot scale.
  • DIM handles most cases automatically; DIMLINEAR, DIMALIGNED, DIMANGULAR for specific ones.
  • Dimension to the object, not to another dimension, so it updates when the object changes.
  • Put dimensions outside the drawing where possible, and never duplicate the same dimension twice — contradictions on site cause expensive mistakes.
  • MTEXT for notes, LEADER for pointing at something.

autocad.title: Blocks and a floor plan project
autocad.summary: Reusable components, and drawing a complete plan from start to finish.
autocad.html:
Blocks

A block is a set of objects saved as one named item. Doors, windows, toilets, chairs, title blocks, north arrows.

  • BLOCK (B) — select objects, name it, pick a sensible base point (the hinge of a door, the centre of a column).
  • INSERT (I) — place copies, with scale and rotation.
  • Edit the block definition once and every instance updates. That is the point of them.
  • WBLOCK writes a block out as its own file so you can reuse it across projects. Build a personal library — it is the biggest speed gain available to you.

Draw blocks on layer 0; they then take on the layer they are inserted into.

Floor plan project

A two-bedroom house. Work in millimetres.

  1. Set up — UNITS to decimal, create your layers, set dimension style.
  2. Grid lines — draw the structural centre lines first on a Centre layer.
  3. Walls — draw one face, OFFSET by 200 for the thickness. Use FILLET with radius 0 to clean the corners.
  4. Openings — offset lines to mark where doors and windows go, then TRIM the wall between them.
  5. Insert blocks — doors with swings, windows, sanitary ware.
  6. Rooms — text for names, and areas.
  7. Dimensions — an overall string outside, then a string for room sizes, then openings.
  8. Hatch — H for wall poche or floor finishes. Set the scale so it reads at plot size; a hatch that looks solid is scaled wrong.
  9. Title block — project, client, scale, date, drawing number, revision.

Checking

Before issuing: do the dimensions add up to the overall? Does every door have a swing that does not hit something? Is anything on the wrong layer? Zoom to extents and look for stray objects miles from the drawing — they ruin plotting.

autocad.title: 3D modelling, plotting and printing to scale
autocad.summary: Moving into three dimensions, and getting paper out that a builder can use.
autocad.html:
3D basics

Switch the workspace to 3D Modelling and set the view to SE Isometric to see depth.

  • EXTRUDE — push a closed 2D shape into a solid. A wall outline becomes a wall.
  • PRESSPULL — the quick version: click inside a closed area and drag.
  • REVOLVE — spin a profile around an axis for anything turned, like a bottle or column.
  • UNION, SUBTRACT, INTERSECT — combine solids. Subtract a box from a wall to cut a window.
  • UCS — move the drawing plane so you can draw on a vertical face. Essential, and the part that takes practice.

ORBIT (hold Shift and the scroll wheel) turns the model. Use Visual Styles to switch between wireframe and shaded.

Only model what you need. A full 3D model of a whole building takes far longer than the 2D drawings it produces, and clients usually pay for the drawings.

Layouts and plotting

This is where most beginners struggle, and it is simple once the idea lands:

  • Model space — you draw at full size, always.
  • Layout (paper space) — represents the sheet of paper. Set it to A3, A2 or A1.
  • A viewport in the layout is a window onto the model, and the viewport carries the scale.
  1. Open a Layout tab, right-click it › Page Setup, choose your printer and paper size.
  2. MVIEW to create a viewport.
  3. Double-click inside it to enter, then set the scale from the status bar — 1:50 or 1:100 for plans.
  4. Lock the viewport so a stray scroll does not change the scale.
  5. Put the title block and any notes in paper space, not in the model.

Plot settings

  • Plot style — monochrome.ctb for black and white drawings, which is what most site prints want.
  • Lineweights come from layer colours through the plot style table.
  • Always Preview before plotting. It shows exactly what comes out.
  • Export to PDF for sending — DWG to PDF keeps it vector and scaled, so a contractor can measure off it.

Write the scale on the drawing and add a scale bar. Prints get photocopied at the wrong size, and a scale bar survives that.

mobile-app-development.title: How apps work, Dart, and your first screen
mobile-app-development.summary: Setting up Flutter, the language basics, and widgets.
mobile-app-development.html:
How a mobile app is put together

Almost every app is three parts: a front end the user touches, a back end holding shared data, and the network between them. Flutter builds the front end for Android and iOS from one codebase — which is why it is worth learning first.

Setting up

  1. Install the Flutter SDK and add it to your PATH.
  2. Install Android Studio for the Android SDK and an emulator.
  3. Install VS Code with the Flutter and Dart extensions — lighter for day-to-day work.
  4. Run flutter doctor and fix every warning before writing code. It will tell you exactly what is missing.
  5. flutter create my_app, then flutter run.

Test on a real phone over USB with developer options enabled. Emulators are slow on modest laptops, and a real device shows you real performance.

Dart, quickly

  • var infers the type; final is set once; const is fixed at compile time.
  • Types: int, double, String, bool, List, Map.
  • Null safety — String? may be null, String may not. The compiler forces you to handle it, which prevents the most common crash in mobile apps.
  • Functions: int add(int a, int b) => a + b;
  • Classes with named constructors and async/await for anything that takes time.

Everything is a widget

Text, a button, padding, the whole screen — all widgets, nested in a tree.

  • StatelessWidget — never changes after it is built.
  • StatefulWidget — holds data that changes; call setState() and Flutter rebuilds it.
  • Scaffold gives you the page structure: appBar, body, floatingActionButton.
  • MaterialApp wraps everything and carries the theme and routes.

Use hot reload (r in the terminal, or save in VS Code). Changes appear in under a second with the app's state intact. It changes how you learn.

mobile-app-development.title: Layouts, lists, navigation and forms
mobile-app-development.summary: Building screens that hold real content and move between each other.
mobile-app-development.html:
Layout

  • Column stacks vertically, Row horizontally.
  • mainAxisAlignment positions along the direction of the Column or Row; crossAxisAlignment across it.
  • Expanded makes a child take the remaining space; Flexible lets it shrink.
  • Container for padding, margin, colour and borders; Padding and SizedBox when that is all you need.
  • Stack layers widgets on top of each other, positioned with Positioned.

The infamous "RenderFlex overflowed" yellow stripes mean a Column is taller than the screen. Wrap it in SingleChildScrollView, or use Expanded. You will meet this on day one.

Lists

ListView.builder is the one to use — it builds only the visible rows, so a list of ten thousand items scrolls smoothly.

Give it itemCount and an itemBuilder that returns a widget for each index. ListTile gives you a standard row with leading icon, title, subtitle and trailing widget.

For a grid, GridView.builder works the same way.

Navigation

  • Navigator.push(context, MaterialPageRoute(builder: (_) => DetailScreen())) opens a screen.
  • Navigator.pop(context) goes back, and can return a value to the screen that opened it.
  • Named routes declared in MaterialApp keep larger apps tidy.
  • BottomNavigationBar or TabBar for the main sections.

Forms and input

  • TextField with a TextEditingController to read what was typed. Dispose the controller in dispose() or you leak memory.
  • Wrap fields in a Form with a GlobalKey<FormState>, use TextFormField with a validator, and call _formKey.currentState!.validate() on submit.
  • Set keyboardType — a phone number field should open the number pad.
  • Show errors under the field, never in an alert. And show a loading state on the button while submitting, or people tap twice.

mobile-app-development.title: State, APIs and local storage
mobile-app-development.summary: Managing data that changes, fetching it from a server, and keeping it on the device.
mobile-app-development.html:
State management

State is any data that changes while the app runs. setState() is fine for a single screen. The problem comes when two distant screens need the same data — passing it down through every widget in between gets unbearable.

  • Provider — the sensible next step and the easiest to learn. A ChangeNotifier holds the data, calls notifyListeners() when it changes, and any widget reading it rebuilds.
  • Riverpod — the modern successor, testable and compile-safe.
  • BLoC — heavier, used on large team projects.

Start with setState, move to Provider when it hurts. Do not reach for the most complex option first.

Calling an API

Add the http package. The shape is always the same:

  1. await http.get(Uri.parse(url)).
  2. Check response.statusCode == 200.
  3. jsonDecode(response.body) into a Map or List.
  4. Convert into your own model class with a fromJson factory constructor.

Use FutureBuilder to render the three states the user can actually be in: waiting (spinner), hasError (a message and a retry button), and data (the list). Apps that only handle the happy path feel broken on a slow connection — which in Uganda is most of the time.

Always wrap network calls in try/catch and set a timeout. Never leave a spinner running forever.

Local storage

  • shared_preferences — small values: a token, a setting, whether onboarding was seen.
  • sqflite — a real SQL database on the device, for structured records.
  • Hive — fast key-value storage for objects, no SQL needed.

Cache the last successful API response and show it when offline. An app that shows yesterday's data beats an app that shows an error.

Never store passwords in shared_preferences. Use flutter_secure_storage for tokens, and keep API keys and secrets on your server, never in the app — anything shipped in an APK can be extracted.

mobile-app-development.title: Theming, testing, and publishing to the Play Store
mobile-app-development.summary: Making it look like yours, checking it works, and getting it live.
mobile-app-development.html:
Theming

Define the look once in MaterialApp's theme: rather than styling each widget.

  • ColorScheme.fromSeed(seedColor: ...) generates a full, accessible palette from one brand colour.
  • Set textTheme, elevatedButtonTheme and inputDecorationTheme so every button and field matches without repetition.
  • Provide a darkTheme too; many people run their phones dark.
  • Add custom fonts through google_fonts or the assets section of pubspec.yaml.

Check your contrast. Light grey text on white is unreadable outdoors in daylight, which is where your users are.

Testing and debugging

  • Unit tests for logic, widget tests for screens, integration tests for full journeys. Run with flutter test.
  • Flutter DevTools — the widget inspector shows why your layout is wrong far faster than guessing.
  • Test on a low-end Android phone, not only an emulator. Test with slow data and with data off.
  • Test both a small screen and a tablet.

Preparing for release

  1. Set the applicationId in android/app/build.gradle — e.g. com.yourbusiness.appname. It can never be changed after publishing.
  2. Set the app name and icon (flutter_launcher_icons makes every size for you).
  3. Create a keystore and configure signing. Back the keystore up. Lose it and you can never update the app again — you would have to publish a new one and lose your users.
  4. flutter build appbundle — the Play Store wants an .aab, not an APK.

Publishing

  • A Google Play developer account is a one-off USD 25.
  • You will need: screenshots on several screen sizes, a 512×512 icon, a feature graphic, a short and full description, and a privacy policy URL — mandatory, even for a simple app.
  • Complete the Data Safety form honestly, declaring what you collect.
  • Publish to internal testing first, get real people using it, then promote to production.
  • Review takes days, sometimes longer. Plan launches around that, and expect at least one rejection — read the reason, fix it, resubmit.

After launch, watch the crash reports and the reviews. The first update usually matters more than the release, because it fixes what real users hit.
